The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2684. Nations Championship schedule, results, kick-off times and how to watch

Rugby's Nations Championship bursts back into life as the inaugural edition comes to a conclusion in a busy November.

The new competition pits the Six Nations sides against the four Rugby Championship competitors, plus Japan and Fiji, across six matches split evenly across the July and November Test windows.

The results of those games will determine each of the 12 teams' seedings for the finals weekend at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium, with six matches contested over two days and both team and hemisphere silverware up for grabs.

Each entrant will be matched against the equivalent qualifier from the other pool to decide overall placings at the conclusion of a busy year of international action. South Africa and New Zealand are assured of a top-two finish in their pool – with the All Blacks given a huge opportunity to seize the initiative after the Springboks were beaten by France.

Here's the full competition schedule, and how it will all work:

Announced during the 2023 Rugby World Cup, the new competition will be held every other year and replaces the traditional summer tours and Autumn Nations Series. It is designed to add context to the international calendar, with Fiji and Japan invited to join the Six Nations and Rugby Championship sides to form a top 12. Promotion and relegation is planned for the future with the second-tier Nations Cup, though will not take place in 2026.

Northern Hemisphere: France, Ireland, Scotland, Italy, England, Wales.

Southern Hemisphere: South Africa, New Zealand, Argentina, Australia, Fiji, Japan.

The first finals weekend will be held at Twickenham on the last weekend (27 to 29) of November. Three days of double-headers will be held at the ground, with the first-placed finisher of the Six Nations sides meeting whoever tops the other pool, and so on and so forth down the rankings.

The winner of that marquee match will lift the first Nations Championship trophy, while whichever hemisphere – a term used loosely with Japan included in the "southern" section and Fiji hosting their games in the United Kingdom – wins more final matches will also be crowned. The 1st vs 1st match is worth two points, with all other matches in the finals weekend worth one.

Viewers in the United Kingdom will be able to watch every game on ITV after the free-to-air broadcaster struck a deal to show the competition.

Scotland vs Australia (3.10pm, Edinburgh)

England vs New Zealand (2.10pm, Twickenham)

Eleventh place final (4.40pm): Northern 6 vs Southern 6

Fifth place final (8.10pm): Northern 3 vs Southern 3

Ninth place final (1.10pm): Northern 5 vs Southern 5

Third place final (4.40pm): Northern 2 vs Southern 2

Seventh place final (1.10pm): Northern 4 vs Southern 4

Nations Championship final (4.40pm): Northern 1 vs Southern 1

#2681. Vikings-Packers Final Injury Report

The Minnesota Vikings and Green Bay Packers released their final injury reports, along with injury designations, in advance of their matchup on Sunday at Lambeau Field. Here they are:

PUP = Physically unable to participate list.

IR = Injured reserve. Note: only starters on IR are listed.

Probable = the league defines a Probable injury designation as a 75% or greater chance of playing. Historically, 95% of players designated probable are active and played on game day.

Questionable = the league defines a Questionable injury designation as being 'uncertain' of whether the player will play or not. This replaces the former definition of having a 50% chance of playing. Historically, 70-75% of players with a Questionable injury designation were active and played on game day.

Doubtful = The league defines a Doubtful injury designation to mean the player is unlikely to participate in the game. In practical terms, teams use the designation when a player has less than a 50% chance to suit up, and active game appearances from this designation remain rare. Historically only around 6% of players with a Doubtful designation are active and played on game day.

Out = will not play. Players with this designation are not active on game day and league rules prohibit them from playing.

For the Vikings, kind of the worst-case scenario based on the injury list earlier this week, with only Kyle Van Noy being upgraded today among previous DNP players- the rest of which are out on Sunday, including Blake Cashman, T.J. Hockenson, Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins, Jauan Jennings, and Kyler Murray. Moreover, Jordan Addison and Josh Metellus were added to the injury report as both were limited on Friday and carry questionable injury designations. Hopefully both will be able to go on Sunday, however. Not having Hockenson will make it a bit tougher for the debut of Kirk Cousins on Sunday while not having Blake Cashman means Eric Wilson may have the green dot on defense on Sunday with a greater role for Ivan Pace Jr. and probably Jake Golday as well.

For the Packers, starters Josh Jacobs, Sean Rhyan, and Micah Parsons are out, as expected. Starting linebacker Zaire Franklin is doubtful, meaning he probably won't play on Sunday. A few other starters are questionable for the Packers on Sunday, including right guard Kevin Zeitler, defensive end Lukas Van Ness, and safeties Javon Bullard and Xavier McKinney- who was added to the injury list on Friday with a foot injury. Lastly, running back Chris Brooks is also questionable, and with Josh Jacobs out on Sunday may be expected to have more of a role if he's able to go. But while I expect most of the questionable players to play on Sunday for the Packers, most of them have injuries that may keep them at less than 100%.

Overall, both teams are a bit banged up and will be missing some key starters on Sunday.

#2680. Annika 2026: Three players share lead after 36 holes

BELLEAIR, Fla. — Hye-Jin Choi opened with two bogeys, made up ground with a 15-foot eagle putt late and finished with a 3-under 67 Friday that gave her a three-way share of the lead at The Annika and another chance to win for the first time in 127 tries on the LPGA Tour.

It was far more effective than the bogey-free round of Nelly Korda, the No. 1 player who could only laugh at her clean card because it was cleaner than she would have preferred — 15 straight pars, one birdie, two closing pars for a 69.

That left Korda four shots behind going into the week at Pelican Golf Club, where a victory would make the 28-year-old American eligible for the LPGA Hall of Fame.

"I had a lot of chances," said Korda, competing for the first time in two months. "But you can just tell that from yesterday morning to today afternoon with the wind, that's what the defense of this golf course is. It's as fast as Bermuda as I've putted on throughout my career."

It wasn't a problem for Solheim Cup star Carlota Ciganda, who birdied her last four holes for a 63 to join Choi and Lindy Duncan (66) atop the leaderboard at 12-under 128.

The Japanese duo of Mao Saigo (65) and Minami Katsu (69) were two shots behind.

Choi has been an LPGA member for five years and it has been a curious chase for that first LPGA victory, particularly since she was 17 when she had a late lead in the 2017 U.S. Women's Open and wound up as a runner-up.

She also had two good chances at winning during the recent Asia swing, where she was runner-up in Shanghai and South Korea.

The ANNIKA tees off at Pelican Golf Club in Belleair, Fla.

Choi was playing in the group with Korda the opening two rounds, which she believes has tested her enough to calm her nerves on the weekend. She wasn't rattled by the bogey-bogey start, or the bogey on the par-5 14th, her fifth hole of the round.

She pieced together enough birdies to regain some momentum, then hit an approach that got a nice kick around the green and rolled out to just under 15 feet for eagle on the par-5 seventh.

"I have two rounds left, but I have recently played in a champion group on the tournament before, so I have that experience and I'm going just try my best and concentrate on my game like two rounds," Choi said.

Scoring was low enough in the opening round that 1-under 139 made the cut. This is the final regular-season event of the year, and the top 60 in the Race to CME Globe advance to the finale next week in Naples, where the winner gets $2 million.

Julia Lopez Ramirez of Spain, who defeated Yealimi Noh in a crucial singles match in her Solheim Cup debut, was among those at 9-under 131. That was important for the Spaniard, who came into the week at No. 66 in the Race to the CME Globe.

Duncan, the 35-year-old Floridian, has yet to win on the LPGA Tour and this was the first time she had at least a share of the lead through 36 holes. She went 2-1 in her Solheim Cup debut, where she was the oldest first-timer for the Americans since Nancy Scranton was 39 in 2000.

This is her sixth consecutive tournament, and fifth week in a row on a trip that has taken her from Shanghai to South Korea to Malaysia to Japan to the Tampa Bay area. She looked no worse from the wear of traveling and time zones.

"The week has gone by really fast, which is sometimes a good thing," Duncan said. "Because if you're playing a lot and you get some momentum going, that's kind of a nice way to play. So it's just been kind of rolling with it."

Gaby Lopez in contention at Annika after having 'dream come true' dancing on stage with Jason Derulo

The last few days have been eventful for Gaby Lopez. After joining Jason Derulo on stage in Belleair, Florida on Tuesday night, the 33-year-old Mexican star shot a 7-under 63 during the second round to move into contention at the Annika.

#2676. NFL predictions: Can the Falcons slow down Kenneth Walker?

The Falcons had a rough outing in Week 9, falling by two scores to the Cincinnati Bengals in Madrid. Atlanta was able to compete for the first part of the game, but quickly fell behind and ultimately looked outclassed by one of the NFL's premier offenses. That result, and the way it unfolded, seemed to prompt some soul-searching from the Falcons coaching staff and front office. In the ensuing days, Atlanta traded away star safety Jessie Bates III and starting center Ryan Neuzil.

That seems to signal a change in philosophy for the Falcons to more prominently focusing on the future. Atlanta isn't going to tank or anything close to it—the NFC South is led by a 3-win team at the moment, so nobody is even close to being "out of it". But this is at least a tacit acknowledgement that the current construction of the team isn't close enough to turn down future assets. It's the right move, and an important realization for the new staff.

That said, there's still a big game coming up this weekend against the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 10. The Falcons are currently 3.5-point home underdogs, per FanDuel, and there are some significant injury question marks to consider heading into this one.

The biggest matchup to watch here will be the beleaguered Falcons run defense against the electric Chiefs rushing attack headed by former Seahawks star Kenneth Walker. Walker has been a godsend for Kansas City, finding a new level of success beyond even his final Super Bowl-winning season in Seattle. With the Chiefs passing game still a bit lackluster, Walker's dominance on the ground has been a key cog in their offensive machine.

Even though Atlanta started out the season with fantastic run defense, teams have largely figured out how to beat the Falcons attacking-style front with inside runs and a lot of man/gap concepts. The Falcons haven't yet developed a counterpunch, and until they do…it's going to be a long day for the defense against any team with even a semi-competent rushing attack. Slowing down Kenneth Walker—or having him not play, as he's currently questionable for the game—is a pivotal matchup to watch.

On the other side of the ball, the Falcons will have to build some offensive consistency. Michael Penix Jr. is in the midst of a two-game slump and was unable to find much success against a fairly beatable Bengals defense. The bigger issue might be the ground game, which should be the backbone of the offense but hasn't had any consistent success in over a month. With Ryan Neuzil heading out and Corey Levin taking over at center, I'm not expecting significant strides there. But perhaps Levin is a better fit for what Bill Callahan wants to do, given their experience together.

This is a tough matchup for Atlanta against a Super Bowl-contending Chiefs team. I'm not expecting much from the offense or defense, to be completely honest. With a bye coming up in Week 11, I worry we might see a "let's just get to the bye" performance. Hopefully I'm wrong, and the Falcons can at least give us an entertaining game on Sunday. An upset victory would keep Atlanta right in the thick of things in the NFC South, and the latter part of the schedule is considerably easier than the last month and a half. We'll see if the Falcons can do it.

#2675. Washington football among teams impacted by FAA ground stoppage

This post will be updated with new information as it is received.

Ahead of a matchup with Michigan State, the Washington Huskies are among a handful of teams in college football that have been impacted by an FAA equipment outage that has issued a ground stoppage for all flights traveling across the United States on Friday.

"The directive instructs all departing aircraft to remain on the ground until further notice," USA TODAY reported on Friday afternoon. "Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the ground stop followed a communication issue affecting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers."

All planes that are currently in the air will be allowed to land at their destinations, and according to the Seattle Times' Andy Yamashita, Washington's plane barely missed the cutoff window before the stoppage was issued. A Washington spokesperson has since stated that the Huskies have left Boeing Field and returned to campus, where they will await a further update.

As of 3:00 p.m. PT, the FAA's website reads that the ground stoppage at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport and Boeing Field, where the Huskies fly out of, is planned until 5:00 p.m. PT. However, that is subject to change before Washington's matchup with the Spartans, which is scheduled for 4:15 p.m. ET/1:15 p.m. PT on Saturday afternoon.

According to a report from ESPN's Pete Thamel, the Huskies are one of three Big Ten teams affected by the outage, along with Minnesota and Purdue; however, the Boilermakers will reportedly take buses to Iowa. Washington does not have that same luxury.

It's unclear whether the Big Ten will offer any alternatives.

#2671. Clay Holmes Free Agency: Five Landing Spots For The Starter

Clay Holmes is back on the market, and the deal looks different this time. The former Yankees closer has successfully turned himself into a starting pitcher. After throwing 101 1/3 innings for the Chicago Cubs and New York Mets, he turned down his $12 million player option for 2027. A fractured right fibula stopped his season in May, but he returned in August to make nine starts for Chicago, according to Just Baseball. Beyond the top-tier names on the market, franchises now view him as a reliable rotation choice.

His numbers show a pitcher who limits damage rather than striking out everyone. Holmes posted a 3.29 ERA last season with a 3.63 FIP and a 1.19 WHIP. He gave up only six home runs in 101 1/3 innings. The 33-year-old relies on a sinker that accounts for nearly half his pitches. Just Baseball states that he induced groundballs on 60.8% of batted balls during the previous season. This skill set helps him limit hard contact even when his 18.6% strikeout rate stays low.

Just Baseball predicts Holmes will sign a three-year, $54 million deal with the New York Mets. That works out to an $18 million annual average value. Prior to 2025, he inked a three-year, $38 million deal with the Mets following years spent mostly in relief. New York gave him the chance to start again, a role he had not held regularly since his minor league days. He answered with 165 2/3 innings, a career high, alongside a 3.53 ERA in 31 starts. The Mets know his stuff, and they know he can handle the innings.

Other clubs might offer more money, but the fit is clear. Relying on his sinker to prevent batters from lifting the ball, Holmes extended his success into 2026. His changeup held opponents to a .186 average, while his sweeper allowed just a .154 batting average. Whether teams value his output against his injury record and age will determine his next contract. The Mets are the logical place for him to land again.

Just Baseball projects a contract length of two to four years with an expected annual average value between $16 million and $22 million. Holmes is 34 in 2027, so teams will be cautious about the long term. His 10.0% walk rate also means the defense behind him is crucial for his success. He needs fielders to turn groundballs into outs since he does not miss many bats. A team with a strong infield defense would be the perfect partner for his style.

The injury is the main worry. On May 15, Spencer Jones hit a 111.1 mph comebacker that broke Holmes's right fibula. The ailment removed him from action for almost three months and brought his time in Queens to a close. When the deadline arrived, the Cubs acquired Holmes and outfielder Tyrone Taylor from New York. Despite the setback, his ability to induce groundballs remains his greatest asset. Teams need to decide if the risk is worth the reward of a reliable innings eater.

Several teams need rotation help, and Just Baseball notes Holmes provides an option cheaper than the priciest starters. Before the injury occurred, the right-hander posted a 2.39 ERA over nine starts to begin 2026. His body of work proves he can handle a starter's workload when healthy. The New York Mets remain the top predicted landing spot for the free agent.

#2670. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

Thursday night, Delaware Academy announced that it had been forced to forfeit its Section 4 Class D semifinal win over Deposit/Hancock from this past weekend, removing the state's No. 2-ranked Class D team from its spot in a sectional final this weekend.

In a letter posted to the district's Facebook page, Delaware Academy Central School District at Delhi Superintendent Carey Shultz wrote that Section 4 had ruled the Bulldogs must forfeit their semifinal win and the remainder of their 2026 season "due to a sectional eligibility rule we were unaware of."

In the letter, Shultz said that the ruling came in the wake of a similar issue that occurred elsewhere in the state. Earlier this week, the Middletown football team was forced to forfeit its semifinal win in the Section 9 Class AA playoffs and removed from its spot in a sectional championship game after using an ineligible player.

"Prompted by recent news from another school within New York State, the district was reviewing its readiness for the upcoming sectional final when we learned our team would not be able to advance," Shultz wrote. "Section IV's ruling is based on its eligibility requirements for teams entering sectional play."

Under state rules, football players must be considered an eligible participant for a minimum of three regular season games to be eligible for postseason competition

Delaware Academy had a 9-1 record following its 49-14 semifinal win over Deposit/Hancock and had been scheduled to play Tioga in the sectional final. In his letter, Shultz noted that the Delaware Academy district has filed an appeal of Section 4's decision and that the championship game has been pushed back to Sunday "to allow time for the appeal to be reviewed."

In a follow-up letter posted Friday afternoon on the district's Facebook page, Shultz wrote that Section 4 upheld its original decision, but noted that the district "is in the process of pursuing future remedies," and has requested assistance through state Sen. Peter Oberacker's office while also making an additional appeal through the New York State Public High School Athletic Association.

Meanwhile, according to reports from multiple media outlets, the Enlarged City School District of Middletown withdrew its petition to get its spot in Saturday's Section 9 Class AA championship game against Newburgh Free Academy restored following a hearing Friday in state Supreme Court in Orange County.

The Middie Bears had a perfect 10-0 record after their 48-15 semifinal victory over Valley Central this past weekend, but were removed from the postseason earlier this week when they were forced to forfeit that game due to using an ineligible player.

According to court documents, the unnamed player in question was a member of the Middletown boys' soccer program who joined the football program as a kickoff specialist late in the season. The player appeared in one regular-season game and was listed as an eligible participant - but was not in uniform - for another, then appeared in the sectional semifinal.

The Middletown district, which referred to the issue as an "unintentional adult error in understanding the rules" in a letter posted to the district website, had a waiver request denied by Section 9 and an appeal denied by NYSPHSAA. Local officials weighed in with letters of support, and a Change.org petition started in support of the Middletown team had nearly 6,500 signatures as of late Friday morning.

On Wednesday, the district filed a petition in state Supreme Court in Orange County seeking emergency relief. The hearing was held Friday before Judge Verris B. Shako.

NYSPHSAA, in its response to the petition, noted that Middletown athletic director Justin Sturge was in attendance at a mandatory workshop for Section 9 athletic directors earlier this year where the rule "was clearly explained," and that a Monroe County court upheld the rule in a similar case in 2014 when Aquinas Institute was forced to forfeit its spot in the Section 5 postseason when a quarterback who had only participated in two games prior to sectional playoffs was ruled ineligible.

Valley Central and Newburgh Free Academy are now set to play for the Section 9 Class AA championship on Saturday at noon at Monroe-Woodbury final. The Section 9 champion will play the Section 2 Class AA champion - either Saratoga Springs or CBA - in the regional playoffs next week.

A third sectional championship game that had been in doubt, the Section 5 Class B game between Honeoye Falls-Lima and East/World of Inquiry School, will proceed as scheduled on Saturday despite prior concerns that East/World of Inquiry would be forced to forfeit in the wake of a bench-clearing incident after the final whistle of its semifinal win over James Monroe.

Section 5 officials announced Wednesday that, following an investigation by the Rochester City School District and a review by both Section 5 and NYSPHSAA, multiple East/WOIS players "were misidentified as a disqualified player." East/WOIS will face Honeoye Falls-Lima for the sectional title on Saturday at 3 p.m. at St. John Fisher University.

This article originally published at Delaware Academy removed from Section 4 football final over player eligibility; Middletown drops appeal ahead of Section 9 final.

#2663. Group of retired MLB umpires, including Joe West, file lawsuit alleging they are owed more than $2 million

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former MLB umpire Joe West is part of a group of five retired umpires who are suing their pension plan and alleging they have been underpaid by the plan, the Associated Press reports. West, along with Tom Hallion, Gerry Davis, Larry Vanover, and Jerry Layne, filed the suit in late September in federal court in New York.

The suit alleges that the five umpires have been underpaid by the pension plan by more than $2 million. According to the AP, the suit "was filed against the American Leagues and National Leagues of Professional Baseball Clubs Retirement Income Plan for Umpires and that entity's retirement committee." The five umpires claim their benefits were not calculated correctly and therefore should receive additional money.

West, 74, retired from umpiring in MLB in 2021 after umpiring more than 5,000 games at the highest level starting in 1976. The man they called "Cowboy Joe" umpired a record 5,460 games in all, was known as a colorful figure in the sport and sometimes even a source of controversy.

In 2021, West won more than $500,000 in damages as the result of a defamation suit against former MLB player Paul Lo Duca after Lo Duca alleged during a podcast that West would "open up the strike zone" for reliever Billy Wagner in exchange for driving one of Wagner's vintage cars.

West referenced his "history with lawsuits" on Thursday. From the AP:

West said that when he brought up the issue to the retirement committee, he was offered a relatively small sum. West said MLB senior vice president and chief employment counsel Steven Gonzalez told him: "If you don't like the number, sue us."

"Does Steve Gonzalez not know my history with dealing with lawsuits?" West said.

Like West, Davis also retired after the 2021 season while Hallion umpired through the 2022 season and Layne and Vanover stepped away after the 2024 campaign. The five sued as individuals and did not involve the umpires' union, their lawyer, Paul B. Holmes, said, per the AP.

A pretrial conference in the case is scheduled for Dec. 11.

#2660. Ex-Guardians catcher Bo Naylor testifies in defense of Emmanuel Clase, Luis Ortiz in MLB pitch-rigging trial

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former Cleveland Guardians catcher Bo Naylor on Thursday testified in federal court that he perceived nothing untoward about disputed pitches thrown by former All-Star closer Emmanuel Clase and his former Guardians teammate Luis Ortiz, ESPN reports.

Naylor, who played five seasons for the Guardians, appeared as a witness for the defense in the ongoing federal trial in which prosecutors allege that Clase and Ortiz rigged multiple pitches for the benefit of co-conspiring bettors. In Clase's case, he's alleged to have done so in 17 games across a two-year period beginning in May 2023. Naylor, now a member of the Milwaukee Brewers, was catcher for some of Clase's disputed appearances during that span, including seven of the 18 pitches he's alleged to have rigged.

Naylor, a defense witness, was shown video replays of some of the pitches the government alleges were predetermined by Clase or Ortiz as part of the scheme. Naylor was behind the plate for many of them and said they looked like common sliders outside the strike zone. He said the scouting reports on the hitters Ortiz faced during the two pitches in question indicated that sliders low and away would be a "weapon."

In November 2025, Clase and Ortiz were indicted by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of New York. According to the Department of Justice, both pitchers "agreed in advance with their co-conspirators to throw specific types of pitches and speeds of pitches." The Department of Justice alleged that the pair made at least $450,000 by rigging outings and throwing specific pitches to benefit bettors who wagered on the outcomes of those pitches.

Both Clase and Ortiz pleaded not guilty to those charges in November of last year. Clase and Ortiz have been on administrative leave since late June 2025 while Major League Baseball investigates. MLB has the authority to discipline the pitchers regardless of how the criminal trial plays out.

The pair could face up to 65 years in prison if convicted on the charges of wire fraud conspiracy, honest services wire fraud conspiracy, conspiracy to influence sporting contests by bribery, and money laundering conspiracy.

#2656. Five under-the-radar MLB free agents who could make a big impact next season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a little more than a week old now and we're still waiting for the first big trade or free agent signing. That isn't unusual, though. The hot stove, like the regular season, is a marathon, not a sprint. A lockout is expected when the collective bargaining agreement ends at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and there should be a flurry of activity before then.

We ranked the offseason's top 50 free agents, and although it is not a great class, there are dozens of quality players available. You just have to know where to look. Here now are five players who did not rank among our top 50 free agents, but would nonetheless be good options and solid pickups for teams that want to raise their floor and improve their supporting cast.

It was a tale of two seasons for the 29-year-old Bryan Abreu, who had a 5.81 ERA before the All-Star break and a 1.71 ERA after. The under-the-hood estimators, like FIP and xERA, were better in the second half as well, though Abreu lost close to 2 mph off his fastball this year and, not coincidentally, a whole bunch of swings and misses. Abreu is third in appearances and second in innings among relievers since 2022 and it's possible the workload is catching up to him. There's still enough bat-missing ability and late-inning experience here for Abreu to contribute to a contender's bullpen. It just might happen as a seventh-inning guy moving forward, not as the Moment of Truth™ reliever who pitches in the game's biggest moments.

If you're looking for a bottom of the order guy who will take walks and give you 10-15 home runs, that's J.P. Crawford. His defense, specifically his range and arm, has slipped so much in his early 30s that he's no longer a viable shortstop, though he played 33 games at third base this past season. I like him better at second base, but third base works too. Crawford gets on-base at a decent clip and won't strike out excessively, plus he's long been regarded as an excellent teammate and grade-A clubhouse guy. It seems like his time with the Mariners is over and it's for the best. Crawford can go elsewhere, play a new position, and just be part of the lineup rather than one of the faces of the franchise.

Due to injury and ineffectiveness, it looked like Sean Newcomb was on his way out of baseball two years ago. He then reinvented himself as a sinker/curveball guy and carved out a nice second phase to his career as a workhorse utility reliever who won't beat himself with walks (an early career bugaboo) and will limit hard contact in the air. Newcomb, 33, worked at least 90 innings the last two seasons while pitching in every possible role. He closed out games, worked high leverage as a setup guy, soaked up innings in long relief, and opened a few times as well. Newcomb is likely miscast as a go-to bullpen option, though he can be a valuable third or fourth option for a contender. The utility reliever is all the rage these days and Newcomb fits the profile to a T.

Now 35, Emilio Pagán was sensational after returning from a hamstring injury in July, pitching to a 1.88 ERA with 34 strikeouts and only five walks in his final 28 ⅔ innings. The downside is the same as it's always been: Pagán is exceptionally home run prone (career 1.51 HR/9), which is a bad trait for a late-inning reliever who pitches almost exclusively in close games. His fastball remains firm, though, and his splitter is an elite swing-and-miss pitch that allows him to neutralize righties and lefties. As long as you're willing to live with the home run risk, Pagán remains a capable high-leverage reliever, one who is not out of place pitching important innings for a contending team.

Platoon DHs are not the hottest commodity, but Joc Pederson fills the role about as well as anyone in the game. He's a left-handed hitter, so he's on the heavy side of the platoon, and he authored a .245/.338/.496 line with terrific ball-tracking data (exit velocity, etc.) against righties. If you must play him in the field, Pederson can stand in right field or at first base for about six innings before being subbed out for a defensive replacement. He's essentially a bat-only player, though. Pederson will turn 35 in April and he's still a powerful and productive hitter against righties and an elite clubhouse vibes dude.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2653. Jayson Tatum won't give air to Jaylen Brown drama ahead of Celtics-Sixers game: 'Another game on the schedule'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

MILWAUKEE -- Jayson Tatum downplayed Tuesday's showdown between the Boston Celtics and Philadelphia 76ers, which will be the first time that he and former teammate Jaylen Brown will face each other as opponents.

"It's another game on the schedule. It's the Celtics versus the Sixers. In the words of Brad Stevens, they all count as one," Tatum said after putting up 21 points, four rebounds and six assists in a 117-97 win over the Milwaukee Bucks. "This one counted as one. Go get ready for Tuesday. It's a really good team, obviously. Incredible group, great coaching staff, they've been playing really well. So from that standpoint it's gonna be fun. But it's nothing more than Celtics versus Sixers."

Tatum and Brown spent nine seasons together, and led the Celtics to the 2024 championship -- the historic franchise's first since 2008 and record-setting 18th overall -- before the latter was traded to Philadelphia this summer in a blockbuster deal that brought Paul George to Boston.

Much has been made about Tatum and Brown's relationship, or lack thereof, particularly over the last few weeks.

Late last month, Tatum shared his recollection of the trade in an episode of his documentary series, "Summer of Jayson." "I was just as much caught off guard as the rest of the world," he said. In the comment section of the clip online, Brown called "cap."

Shortly after, Tatum tried to shut down any drama by pointing to all that they had accomplished together. "This ain't no f---in' Shaq and Kobe, there's no beef," Tatum said. "It's not about that. It should be more praise, and I understand that don't necessarily sell. Drama gets clicks and views, but I'm not really — that's not my thing."

Brown, on the other hand, played into the drama a few days later. "There's no beef," Brown said. "Jayson comes from a wonderful family. We've accomplished some great things. He's a hell of a basketball player. He's got a great PR team. It's no beef, but it might be a little lamb chop. And some gravy. He should stay ready at all times."

Now, as the first meeting between the former teammates arrives, both have tried to keep the focus on basketball.

"It's nothing to talk about. I mean, he's on his side, I'm on my side," Brown said after the 76ers secured a 127-121 win over the Chicago Bulls on Sunday. "Just playing basketball. Both of us are trying to win, so it's nothing to talk about. Just check the ball up. ... "We'll see how I feel when we get out there, but as of now, I got no emotion towards anything. So I'm just ready to go."

When Tatum asked if he would have a conversation with Brown on Tuesday, his response was a simple "I'm not able to tell the future," before adding that he had "no idea" if any such conversation would have to wait until after the season.

"I just know that it's the Celtics versus the Sixers. Just go out there and do my job and try to get another win," Tatum said. "Get through that, got a game on Wednesday. It's a long season. We got 72 games left. That's just the focus right now."

As for the actual basketball, both players and teams are off to terrific starts. Brown is averaging 22.3 points, 6.7 rebounds and four assists on 47.7% shooting, including 39.2% from 3-point range, for the 9-2 Sixers, who sit atop the Eastern Conference. Tatum, meanwhile, is at 27.1 points, six rebounds and 7.8 assists for the 8-2 Celtics, who are alone in second.

#2648. NBA's biggest winners and losers of the week: Luka's Lakers look amazing, are Hornets regretting LaMelo trade?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

At the risk of tempting fate, we're coming off of a pretty optimistic week in the NBA. The late-October rush of season-altering injuries has seemingly slowed down. The quality of basketball has been excellent, and stars are making history. Things in the NBA are so positive right now that there are multiple, ongoing seven-game winning streaks that won't be featured in our winners of the week.

So... who beat out the trimmed-for-space Golden State Warriors and San Antonio Spurs? And who are our losers in a week full of winners? Let's dive into our rankings from the week that was.

No Jalen Williams. No Cason Wallace. No Chet Holmgren. And also, no losses. That's the week that the Thunder just had, first sweeping their season series with the Cleveland Cavaliers before blowing the doors off of the Memphis Grizzlies and Washington Wizards by 70 combined points. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander averaged just under 36 points in the 4-0 stretch, but the story here is Oklahoma City finding a new formula to compensate for all of these absences.

The Thunder built their historic defense around turnover generation, leading the NBA on that front in their 2025 championship season and finishing No. 2 a year ago. They've fallen to 21st as of Sunday, accepting that they simply cannot play as aggressively without their core defenders as they once did. Instead, they're selling out to protect the basket. They allowed the second-fewest points in the paint per game a season ago ... and have trimmed five of them off of their average this season. They've even started Isaiah Hartenstein and Aday Mara together in two of their past three games, though they've shared minimal possessions.

The defense may not be generating turnovers, but the offense isn't committing any either. Oklahoma City has taken its turnover-prevention offense to the extreme. The Thunder are averaging 231.6 passes per game, 10 fewer than any team in the tracking era. Only the Spurs and the Philadelphia 76ers, both healthy championship contenders, are turning the ball over less. This "no passes means no turnovers" offense only works if the individual creators are up to snuff. Gilgeous-Alexander obviously fits the bill, but now, so does Ajay Mitchell. The Thunder are scoring over 1.2 points per possession when Mitchell shoots out of pick-and-roll, good for the 94th percentile league-wide. He's scoring just under 25 points per 36 minutes, more than Cade Cunningham and just below Deni Avdija and Austin Reaves.

Oh yeah, and they made a trade with the Sacramento Kings. I'm comfortable calling any team lucky enough to trade with the Kings an automatic winner for that week, especially when they're acquiring a guard on a rookie contract. Do the words "Tyrese Haliburton" mean nothing to you, Sacramento? Nique Clifford certainly won't live up to that prematurely dealt King, but there's a parallel here to Davion Mitchell, another former first-round pick the Kings dealt who has since blossomed with the Miami Heat. You should trust no team's ability to evaluate players less than Sacramento's ... and no team's more than Oklahoma City's. If Sam Presti thinks Clifford can help the injury-ravaged Thunder, I'm inclined to believe that a price of two second-round picks is a bargain. All in all, it was about as perfect a week as the Thunder could have asked for.

He's averaging 40 points! This isn't a handful of games against terrible teams anymore. The Portland Trail Blazers have been great defensively against everyone except the Los Angeles Lakers because Luka has blitzed them for 94 points in two meetings. Of the 20 highest individual point totals so far this season, Dončić comes in at No. 1, No. 2, No. 5, No. 12, No. 17 and No. 18. The two biggest pillars of the MVP race are scoring and winning. Clearly, he's got the scoring down.

So far, winning hasn't been an issue either. The Lakers are 9-2, and it's almost exclusively because of the offense he runs. As of Sunday, the Lakers ranked 23rd in rebounding rate, 23rd in defense and 25th in turnover rate. It hasn't mattered because the offense is No. 1 with a bullet. The Lakers are roughly 34 points per 100 possessions better when he plays than when he sits, yet they were still able to pull off a critical road win over the Detroit Pistons on Sunday without him. The Lakers are a regular-season wins machine, and Dončić is the engineer.

It's not just the raw total, either. It's how this is all happening. Dončić currently leads the NBA in both 3-point attempts and free-throw attempts. When James Harden was doing that a decade ago, it was considered such witchcraft that defenders started standing behind him and guarding him with their hands behind their backs. I look forward to seeing what sort of nonsense teams concoct against Dončić if this continues. He's making 30-footers look like layups. He's giving Laker fans the sort of individual offense they haven't seen since Kobe Bryant's peak. Enjoy it. Stretches like this don't come around often.

The underlying message of the Ball trade was that the Charlotte Hornets did not think he could be relied upon as a franchise player. Given the questions surrounding his durability, his defense and even his maturity, it wasn't a crazy thought. The idea that he would fare better in a secondary role in Minnesota made plenty of sense. He and Anthony Edwards looked like one of the NBA's best duos in the season's opening week. Then Edwards got hurt, and Ball was suddenly back to being the centerpiece. How has he responded? Well, let's look at the team numbers since Edwards went down:

It's a tiny sample, but thus far, Ball is impacting his new Timberwolves teammates in much the same way he affected his former Hornets (don't worry, we'll get to them!). Everyone else's life gets vastly simpler on offense when they're fortunate enough to play with LaMelo Ball. Even without Edwards, he's more than kept the Timberwolves afloat. When Edwards eventually returns, this team is a genuine contender in the Western Conference.

With Ball, the Hornets had the best offense in the NBA from early December through the end of last season. Well, without him, they're last. By a mile. They're last in basically everything. No team has a lower true shooting percentage. No team turns the ball over. Ready for a jarring stat? We covered Oklahoma City's "no pass" offense earlier. Well, the Thunder are averaging more assists than the Hornets this season ... on 65 fewer passes per game.

The Hornets knew they were getting worse when they made the trade. It was a conscious choice: take a step back, take a few spins in the revamped lottery, accumulate assets that could be flipped later. The Hornets felt like they were destined to be a perpetual middle-of-the-standings team with Ball. They traded him in the hopes that getting worse now could make them championship contenders later.

Their fans probably could have lived with a small step back. What we've seen thus far has been a disaster. Not all of it is their fault. They've barely had Coby White or Kon Knueppel -- and Knueppel will be about another four weeks at least with a hamstring strain. Brandon Miller, the other cornerstone here who just signed a $209 million contract, is shooting 26% from 3 and below 36% from the floor because of how overburdened he currently is. A step back may have been the idea, but nobody thought it would be this bad, nor did many assume Ball would be this good for Minnesota. It doesn't change Charlotte's long-term outlook, but it makes the present that much more painful. All of the goodwill from last year's turnaround has seemingly evaporated.

We came into the season relatively certain about how the Western Conference was tiered. The Spurs and Thunder were at the top. The Lakers, the Wolves, the Houston Rockets and the Denver Nuggets would land between No. 3 and No. 6 in some order. After that? Well, no one gave much thought to the Play-In Tournament. The East was supposed to be the deep conference. That's an opinion we cycle through every four or five years. Every year is supposed to be the East's year, and then it isn't. When the Memphis Grizzlies and Portland Trail Blazers were lighting on the world on fire, it seemed as though the West's depth had triumphed yet again.

It still is, on balance. The Warriors and the Dallas Mavericks, for instance, are strongly exceeding expectations. But the early excitement over Memphis and Portland, at least, is starting to wane. The Grizzlies traded a six-game winning streak for a three-game losing streak. The Blazers walked into the hardest stretch of their schedule thus far, took a loss to the Lakers and then got smacked around by the Spurs. With two games against the Thunder coming, Portland is seemingly coming back down to Earth. For a moment there, the New Orleans Pelicans looked as though they were figuring some things out on a four-game winning streak, but back-to-back losses have them out of the Play-In picture, at least for now.

These teams are still better than we figured they'd be, and there's still a bit of wiggle room in the West. Denver, for instance, looks enormously vulnerable. But the Spurs have won eight in a row. The Thunder have righted the ship. The Lakers, Wolves and Rockets are all as good as we thought or better. For a moment there, it looked like we were due some surprises out West. For now, it seems as though order has mostly been restored.

It is still much, much too early to draw any meaningful conclusions about lottery reform, but an early topic thus far this season has been how bad the bottom of the league still is despite the removal of the tanking incentive. With almost three weeks in the books, there are seven teams with either one or two victories. Between those seven teams, there are only three total victories over teams above .500. The Kings beat the Mavericks ... without Kyrie Irving. The Orlando Magic beat the Toronto Raptors ... without Kawhi Leonard, and their victory over the New York Knicks at least came with Jalen Suggs in the lineup. If Suggs and Paolo Banchero were healthy, the Magic would likely not be in this class.

Essentially, when the worst teams are playing against the best ones at anything resembling full strength, they've been hopeless. Inevitably, a certain number of teams is just going to be bad whether or not they're trying to lose. In fact, given this year's specific outlook, it's not even clear how motivated any of these bottom-tier teams are to actually win. The relegation zone isn't a threat to the Milwaukee Bucks, Brooklyn Nets, Utah Jazz or Los Angeles Clippers because they don't actually control their own first-round picks. You could argue that being in the relegation zone would actually be advantageous to the Chicago Bulls in order to minimize their odds of getting a top-five pick in the bad 2027 draft, because doing so, in concert with their No. 4 pick in 2026, would lock them out of a top-five pick in the stronger 2028 class.

We might not see the sort of overt tanking we've gotten in years past, but the question here is whether or not that will actually matter. With so many of these teams having minimal incentives to win, will they still shut down key players midway through the season? Even if they don't, will attendance and television ratings be better for these teams down the stretch just because they're nominally trying? We're months away from even starting to get answers to these questions, but any notions that reform would create 30 competitive teams have been quickly dismissed. Even in October and November, some teams are already pretty tough to watch.

#2647. MLB free agency: Six international players to know for the 2026-27 offseason

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Major League Baseball's free agency period opened earlier this week and teams are now clear to pursue any roster upgrades they deem necessary. That includes players coming over from Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball league, South Korea's Korea Baseball Organization, and Taiwan's Chinese Professional Baseball League. Those are high-level leagues that have sent many impact players MLB's way over the years.

Look no farther than the Dodgers to see how important international talent can be to a club. The Dodgers employed four different former NPB and KBO players this past season, including two-way star Shohei Ohtani, ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and starter Roki Sasaki. Ohtani was signed as an MLB free agent, but the others went to the Dodgers through the posting system.

Per the posting agreement with MLB, posted NPB and CPBL players get a 45-day window to negotiate and sign with an MLB team. KBO players get a 30-day window. Players who do not sign during that posting window return to their previous team in NPB, CPBL, or KBO. The MLB team that signs a posted player pays a fee to the player's former NPB, CPBL, or KBO team.

$5M plus 17.5% of contract value over $25M

$9.375M plus 15% of contract value over $50M

For example, the White Sox paid Munetaka Murakami's former team, the Yakult Swallows, a $6.575 million posting fee on his $34 million contract last offseason. That's $5 million on the first $25 million plus 17.5% of the remaining $9 million, which is $1.575 million. The $5 million plus $1.575 million equals the $6.575 million posting fee paid to the Swallows.

Unlike last lockout, MLB will not be pausing the signing window during the expected lockout, according to The Athletic. In other words, if owners lock players out on Dec. 1 as expected, that date will essentially serve as the same deadline for already posted NPB players unless the lockout ends before their 45-day window expires.

There are no superstar-caliber players like Ohtani or Yamamoto available in this winter's international free agent crop. There are, however, several interesting players who can improve an MLB roster in 2027. Here are the six best NPB, CPBL, and KBO players to know this offseason.

Japan's Triple Crown winner hit .306/.383/.609 with 39 home runs in 2026. He has a similar skill set to Murakami but is not exactly Murakami 2.0. He doesn't have quite as much power (but has plenty of it) and won't walk nearly as often, but he does swing and miss a bunch and is unlikely to remain at the hot corner long-term. Sato is a very aggressive hitter who ran a 66% contact rate this past season. That is below the 77% MLB average. The consensus seems to be that he will land at first base or in a corner outfield spot if not next year, then soon. Murakami successfully overcame his contact issues to slug 35 homers in only 127 games in 2026 around a hamstring injury. At minimum, that will have MLB teams reconsidering how they evaluate the Japan-to-MLB transition. Like Murakami, Sato carries risk, and like Murakami, his power makes that risk worth the dice roll. The Hanshin Tigers officially posted Sato on Nov. 1.

Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man. Taira was officially posted on Nov. 1.

A down 2026 season took some of the shine off Itoh, who won the 2025 Eiji Sawamura Award (Japan's Cy Young equivalent) after throwing 196 ⅔ innings with a 2.52 ERA. To be sure, Itoh pitched well in 2026 (3.18 ERA in 172 ⅔ innings), but he was not as consistently dominant as in the past. The 5-foot-9 right-hander is a seven-pitch pitcher with a low-90s fastball and the usual array of secondary pitches (sinker, cutter, curveball, slider, sweeper, splitter), none of which stands out as a plus offering. Itoh has thrown at least 150 innings in each of the last six seasons. He's seen as a crafty back-end starter in MLB, or perhaps even a reliever (Itoh sat 96 mph out of the bullpen in the World Baseball Classic). The Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters posted Itoh on Nov. 1.

Roh has an unusual agreement with the Hanwha Eagles. He signed the richest deal in KBO history in February (11 years and roughly $23 million), and as part of the deal, the Eagles agreed to post him for MLB teams this offseason, and Roh agreed to return to the Eagles to finish his career when his big-league stint is over. This past season, Roh, 26 in November, authored a .283/.360/.505 batting line with 29 home runs. He has real right-handed power and a good approach at the plate. There are concerns about his propensity to swing and miss as well as his arm at the hot corner. The Eagles formally posted Roh on Nov. 1.

The Seibu Lions posted Takahashi last offseason, but he was unable to find a contract to his liking, so he returned to Japan for another season and threw 148 innings with a 2.64 ERA. Takahashi, 30 in February, is an international free agent now, meaning he does not have to be posted and can instead negotiate at his own pace. More of a ground ball pitcher than a bat-misser, Takahashi sits in the 91-95 mph range with his fastball and has two good secondary pitches in his slider and splitter. He also throws a cutter and curveball. Takahashi is considered a potential innings guy for the back of an MLB rotation.

Tseng pitched for Chinese Taipei in the World Baseball Classic in 2023 and 2026 and he has been one of the CPBL's top relievers the last few years. In 2026, he saved 25 games with a 1.80 ERA and 65 strikeouts in 52 ⅓ innings. Tseng's fastball typically sits in the mid-90s and has run as high as 100 mph in the past, though it has been a few years. His go-to secondary pitch is a breaking ball that needs improvement for Tseng to carve out an MLB career as more than a middle reliever.

#2646. Cardinals name Carson Beck starting QB: Rookie faces Aaron Donald, Myles Garrett in NFL debut

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

If the 2026 NFL season feels like an unprecedented year for unheralded rookie quarterbacks, that's because it is.

With the Arizona Cardinals (3-6) announcing Carson Beck as their starting quarterback for Week 10 against the Los Angeles Rams (5-4), he will now be the third rookie quarterback drafted outside of the first two rounds to start a game this season. The other two were undrafted rookies -- Jalon Daniels of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Joe Fagnano of the Baltimore Ravens. That hasn't happened since 1987.

"You never really know until you get to the live bullets on Sunday, but just the way he goes about his business, whether it's been from OTAs through training camp before he got hurt, seeing him operate in that first half," coach Mike LaFleur said. "Plus, the one possession there in the second half, so obviously we'll know more come next Sunday, but we have all the confidence he's ready to roll."

Beck started the season low on the depth chart, and reflected on how it feels to move so far up in the same year.

"Obviously, having gone from the emergency quarterback at the beginning of the season to last week being the backup to now being the starter, it's been a crazy season," Beck said. "It's really been a welcome to the NFL season, just getting introduced to what the league is and what it can be, but I'm super excited for the opportunity and to have the chance to go play with these guys."

Jacoby Brissett started the year as the starter, was then benched, and was eventually traded to the Baltimore Ravens. Gardner Minshew took over as QB1 was Brissett was demoted and at that time, Beck was promoted from emergency third quarterback to backup. The Minshew injury now leaves Beck to take over after spending the first half of the season learning from his predecessors.

"I think the biggest thing is just watching those two and how they carry themselves and how they handle themselves not only in the meeting room around the coaches, but during the walkthrough, during practice, and during the game," Beck said. "I think that's the biggest thing that you can learn from those guys, of everybody's looking at you as a quarterback, and your attitude has to be right each and every day. The moxie going out there, having confidence, and making everyone around you better."

That "confidence" is not something Beck is worried about. He believes that "confidence is a choice" and having it makes everyone around you better as well.

"When you can choose that, again, you just have to go out there and execute," he said. "You have to go out there and do your thing and you have to go out there and be confident, have swag, and have moxie. Regardless of the circumstances, regardless of anything going on around you, regardless of maybe what happened the play before or maybe thinking about what's going to happen the next play. You have to be in the present moment and that's really all you can do and control."

To kick off the 2026 preseason, Beck completed 15 of his 19 throws for 188 yards and a touchdown against the Carolina Panthers. Beck will also become the fifth quarterback to make his first career start against a duo of pass rushers with 100-plus sacks each when he faces the Rams' duo of Aaron Donald and Myles Garrett.

"Who do they got?" LaFleur said jokingly. "I got no expectations for him except to go out and play his game one play at a time. Go let it rip, go have some fun. Have some fun with your guys."

A depleted group represents Beck's supporting cast, with Michael Wilson (neck) and Kendrick Bourne (tibia) out for the season and Marvin Harrison Jr. traded to the Houston Texans. Fifth-round rookie Reggie Virgil, undrafted veteran Simi Fehoko and Pro Bowl return man Devin Duvernay are the projected starters.

Fortunately, Beck also has the 2025 first-team All-Pro tight end at his disposal in Trey McBride. McBride leads the NFL with 73 catches through Week 9, and he has 11 consecutive games with at least seven catches. Beck also knows a thing or two about feeding his superstar tight end after his years teaming with Brock Bowers at Georgia.

The Miami Heat have gotten off to a slow start to Giannis Antetokounmpo's first season in south Florida, which has led to plenty of discussion about Antetokounmpo's fit with Bam Adebayo and the challenges of building around Giannis.

Among those to chime in on the topic is Antetokounmpo's former coach, Doc Rivers, who struggled to get the most out of the star in Milwaukee and never got Antetokounmpo and Damian Lillard on the same page. Rivers recently offered some critiques of Antetokounmpo, noting he's a difficult star to coach because of his play style and a defiance about changing how he plays.

On Sunday, after the Heat beat the Kings, Antetokounmpo was taken aback when asked about the comments by his former coach.

"You have his number, right? You do. I know you do. You gotta go ask him why he thought that; that's on him," Antetokounmpo told The Athletic. "That's not on me. I gotta focus on my team and what I gotta do and how can I be better and how can I help the team. But like, goddamn. That's crazy. Never let bitterness and pettiness get in front of your goals and dreams, man. For every athlete out there, never let that [happen]. That's insane, but you gotta go ask him why he said what he said. Not me."

Rivers' tenure in Milwaukee was a disaster: he took over for Adrian Griffin in the middle of the 2023-24 season with the Bucks 30-13 and proceeded to go 97-103 in his three years with the Bucks. Given Rivers' history of shifting blame, Antetokounmpo can more easily brush aside his critique as Doc once again finding someone else to blame for his team's shortcomings.

However, while Rivers might not be an infallible messenger, he did have some interesting comments about the challenge of coaching Antetokounmpo this week on The Bill Simmons Podcast.

"He has this great passing ability, but he doesn't necessarily have super IQ at the same time," Rivers said. "It's really a strange thing. And he really has one way. Downhill, forceful. Every play, he wants to force it.

"There's times where I wish he'd do one thing. I wish he'd learn how to execute better," Rivers added. "He's one of those guys, you get a lot of them from the U.S., AAU guys, who have never needed to execute, because they can do it on their own. That doesn't help the team."

It's not surprising that Antetokounmpo would balk at those comments, but viewing from the outside, there certainly seems to be validity to at least some of what Rivers says. Questioning a player's IQ will always understandably irk them, but watching Antetokounmpo play with Lillard and now Adebayo, the criticism of him wanting to attack downhill and not adjusting his play style has been apparent for some time.

What might help the Heat the most here is that, for as stubborn as Antetokounmpo can be, he is also fueled by a desire to prove people wrong. While Rivers may have been unable to get Antetokounmpo to buy into changing his style while playing for him, criticizing the former MVP might lead Giannis to show he can adapt his style purely out of spite.

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The biggest thing hanging over baseball this offseason is obviously the expiration of the CBA and what everyone assumes will be a lockout. Until then, we'll find out the major award winners this coming week, starting with Rookies of the Year on Monday. And, of course, there's the player movement yet to come.

For the latter, let's round up Sunday's rumors right here.

As we saw plenty in 2026, the Dodgers have a very talented rotation with a few injury-prone parts (Tyler Glasnow, Blake Snell, Shohei Ohtani as a pitcher, etc.). As such, this bit of speculative reporting from The Athletic makes a ton of sense:

The Dodgers will need someone who can cover innings in 2027. It's just a matter of how much they can lean on Justin Wrobleski, trust how Emmet Sheehan finished the season (I'd say probably a good amount), how healthy Gavin Stone is (unknown), how ready Jackson Ferris is (he seems close) and if they have enough depth options behind them.

All that to say, the Dodgers will be in on Skubal. If he goes elsewhere, I don't think it's as simple as the Dodgers going after the next highest-ranked starter on the market, such as a Freddy Peralta or a Michael King. I could see them taking a flier on some depth options to soak up innings in anticipation of a quick ramp-up post-lockout, sort of like they did when they signed Tyler Anderson in the run-up to the 2022 season.

Yes, the Dodgers are in on the Tarik Skubal bidding. We all know that. But if they lose out on retaining the two-time Cy Young winner, they may not just continue moving down the list for available starters. Then again, it's hard to ever know exactly what Andrew Friedman is going to spend money on.

As things stand, the Dodgers' rotation has Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Snell, Glasnow, Roki Sasaki and Sheehan, at least until Ohtani is ready to rejoin the fray.

Coming off two straight Wild Card Series losses and sub-90-win seasons, the Red Sox would surely like to take things up a notch for the 2027 season. One way might be to build out the depth of the pitching staff. They'll be "in the market for a back-end starter" and a right-handed reliever "with swing-and-miss capability," according to MassLive.

For the rotation: Sonny Gray hits free agency, but Garrett Crochet will return from a nearly full-season injury. Payton Tolle and Ranger Suárez fill the 2-3 spots, with Jake Bennett solid as the No. 4. That leaves Brayan Bello, Kutter Crawford and Tanner Houck as options for the fifth spot in addition to depth. It doesn't seem dire, but we've seen plenty of times what kind of havoc injuries can wreak.

In the bullpen, lefty Aroldis Chapman returns at closer with Garrett Whitlock and Erik Miller as setup men. Houck missing out on a rotation spot could mean he helps late as well.

#2642. 5 bold NFL predictions for second half of season: Packers take NFC North; Seahawks, Rams miss playoffs

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The second half of the NFL season kicked off on Thursday night, and now that we've hit the back half of the schedule, we're officially on the path to Super Bowl LXI in Los Angeles.

There were quite a few surprises during the first half of the season, including the Browns making it to November with a winning record and the Vikings finishing as the NFL's final undefeated team. As we get ready to head down the stretch, there will probably be a few more surprises, and I'm here to tell you what those surprises are going to be. I'll be making five bold predictions for the second half of the season.

So what's in store for the next nine weeks? Let's get to the predictions.

If someone had made this prediction back in August, they probably would have been laughed off the Internet, but now, it seems like a very real possibility. The Seahawks are the defending champs and the Rams were the preseason Super Bowl favorites, and neither team has quite lived up to the hype.

The surging Rams (5-4) have won three games in a row, but they just lost Puka Nacua to injury, and if you throw in the fact that Davante Adams is also hurt, it's getting to the point where Matthew Stafford might have to throw passes to himself. The Rams have the fourth-most difficult remaining strength of schedule in the NFL, with games still to come against the 49ers, Packers and Chiefs.

As for the Seahawks, quarterback play has hampered their season, and it doesn't look like things are going to get much better on that front. Sam Darnold has struggled all year, and to make matters worse, he's been banged up. Drew Lock has been serviceable during his time on the field, but he doesn't exactly make you feel good about this offense. It's hard to see the QB spot improving, and if it doesn't, the Seahawks could end up missing the playoffs.

Oh, and there's one more thing: These two teams still have to play each other twice, with both games coming over the final three weeks of the season. If one team sweeps that series, that will pretty much eliminate the other team. If they split the series, both teams would have to go at least 5-2 in their seven other games just to get to 10-7. In the NFC this year, there's no guarantee that 10-7 is going to get in the playoffs.

If you look at the NFC North odds right now, the Packers are currently viewed as the long shot to win the division (odds via DraftKings):

The oddsmakers have given up on the Packers, but I have not. Despite having almost no rushing attack, Jordan Love and the Packers have gotten hot over the past few weeks by winning five of their past six games. Their only loss in that span came against the Lions in a 20-17 game where Trey Smack became the first kicker in eight years to miss two field goals from inside 35 yards in a single game. They were a bad kicking performance away from pulling out the win.

On Love's end, he's playing some of the best football of his career. As a matter of fact, he's been so good that CBS Sports NFL Writer Garrett Podell argued this week that Love is the NFL's midseason MVP. On top of that, the Packers defense has been playing at an incredibly high level, and that unit is only going to get better with the expected return of Micah Parsons, which will likely come in Week 12.

Based on how the division has played out this year, the Packers (6-3) will likely have to go 7-1 down the stretch, and this team is talented enough to pull that off.

As things currently stand, the 7-1 Bills have control over the No. 1 seed in the AFC, but I think the Broncos eventually catch them. Not only that, but I think the top seed ends up being decided on Christmas Day in Denver when the Broncos host the Bills. The winner of that game will pick up the all-important head-to-head tiebreaker, and if it's the Broncos, they already have a win over the Jaguars, giving them a head-to-head win over two of the AFC's top teams.

Not to mention, the Broncos have already beaten the Chiefs once, and they could add a head-to-head win over the Steelers when they play Pittsburgh on Black Friday.

The biggest advantage for the Broncos (7-2) is that they have the second-easiest remaining strength of schedule at .426. Of their eight remaining games, they still get to play the Chargers, Dolphins, Jets and Raiders (twice). If they win those five games, that gets them to 12 wins, and at that point, a 14-3 season becomes very possible. I think that would be enough to get them the No. 1 seed for the second straight year. If that happens, it would mark just the second time in franchise history that the Broncos have been the top seed in back-to-back seasons.

If you're wondering what it might take for the NFL to change its playoff format, this might do it.

Heading into Week 10, all four teams in the NFC South have exactly three wins. The Saints and Panthers are technically tied for first place at 3-5 with the Falcons and Buccaneers right behind them at 3-6. There's a very real chance that the winner of this division ends up with a 6-11 record. For that NOT to happen, the Panthers or Saints would have to go at least 4-5 down the stretch, and I'm not sure either team is capable of doing that. The Bucs or Falcons could also get to seven wins, but they have an even smaller margin of error: If they want to get to 7-10, they'll have to go 4-4 down the stretch.

The Panthers and Saints actually play each other in Week 10, so one of those teams will be getting to four wins on Sunday. Even taking that into account, I'm not fully convinced we're going to see either one of them win seven games.

If we don't count the NFL's strike years (1982, 1987), there have been just three teams in NFL history that won their division with seven wins, but NO TEAM has ever won a division with six wins.

If that happens in the NFC South and we also see the NFC East produce a division winner with a bad record, that will pave the way for an 11-6 to possibly get left out of the playoffs. There's a very real chance that every team in the NFC North is going to hit 11 wins, and it won't be surprising if the Seahawks or Rams also hit 11 wins. If you take out the NFC North winner, that leaves four or five 11-win teams battling for three playoff spots.

Since the NFL expanded to a 16-game schedule in 1978, there have only been two instances when an 11-win team missed the playoffs: the 1985 Broncos and the 2008 Patriots. In both instances, there was a division winner that made the playoffs without finishing above .500 (8-8 Browns in 1985, 8-8 Chargers in 2008), and that's what we're likely going to see here.

If a six-win NFC South team ends up winning the division and hosting a playoff game, the NFL might have to go back to the drawing board with its playoff format. In early 2025, the Lions offered a proposal to change the seeding in the playoffs, basing the seeding on each team's final record.

All four division winners would still have gotten in under this proposal, but they wouldn't have been guaranteed a home game. If this prediction pans out, the league might have to revisit the proposal during the upcoming offseason.

The most surprising part of the NFL season so far might be the fact that we still haven't seen a head coach get fired. The last time we made it this deep into the season without a coaching change came all the way back in 2017, when we didn't get our first one until December.

This year, it feels like there are several head coaches on the hot seat heading into the second half of the season, including Steichen, Dan Quinn, Aaron Glenn, Nick Sirianni and you could probably even throw in Jim Harbaugh and Brian Schottenheimer.

When you look at that list, it feels like Steichen has the best chance of being fired first. For one, Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon has already proven that she's willing to fire someone after dumping GM Chris Ballard in October.

At 2-7, it's been an ugly year for the Colts, and they have an upcoming schedule that's built for a firing:

Week 10: DolphinsWeek 11: at TexansWeek 12: GiantsWeek 13: Bye

If the Colts lose to the 1-7 Dolphins, Irsay-Gordon might just decide to pull the trigger and ax Steichen. Even if they win, Steichen might not be safe. If the Colts go 1-2 over the next three weeks and enter their bye at 3-9, Irsay-Gordon might decide to let him go then.

It feels like Steichen's time in Indy is running out.
