#2640. How Paul George is fittingly in perfectly (very) early in his Celtics tenure

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Paul George has been in the NBA since 2011. He's made nine All-Star appearances, six All-NBA Teams and four All-Defensive Teams, and scored nearly 20,000 points. But he knew that he would have to prove himself all over again in Boston after he arrived this summer in a blockbuster trade that sent Celtics icon and fan favorite Jaylen Brown to the Philadelphia 76ers.

"I understand my circumstances. I understand how huge JB was, not only for the organization, but here in the city. So, I didn't take it personal," George said at his introductory press conference, regarding the negative reaction to the trade. "To be honest, they should have a relationship, emotionally, to that trade. But my job is to kind of come into a great opportunity for me."

"It's a new group, a new opportunity," George continued. "I think they're getting someone that's ready to -- not fill the shoes or fill the void of JB -- but I think from a personal standpoint myself, I think I can come in and kind of still keep us in that contention. Give us a chance to win."

It's taken George just a few weeks to earn the trust of Celtics fans and show that he can still contribute to winning.

After pouring in 27 points in a 20-point win over the Milwaukee Bucks on Sunday, George is averaging 20.4 points, 5.2 rebounds, 4.1 assists and a career-high 2.3 steals, while shooting a career-high 42.5% from 3-point range for the 8-2 Celtics, who sit in second place in the Eastern Conference behind the 9-2 Sixers.

Those old rivals will meet Tuesday in a highly anticipated showdown that will be Brown and George's first games against their old teams.

"It'll be great to see those guys and compete against them finally," George said Sunday. "Obviously, Philly was a special place for me. It was a rough, you know, tenure, my two years there, but it'll be special to be in the building."

Ahead of George's return to Philadelphia, let's take a closer look at how he's shined so far in Boston:

"We have a superstar and that's [Jayson Tatum]," George said during his introductory press conference. "I'm not here to steal the shine or reinvent who I am. I'm here to help JT. He's the guy."

As great as Tatum and Brown were together, there was always some underlying tension over their place in the organization. Brown, who was named Eastern Conference Finals MVP and Finals MVP in 2024 when the Celtics won the title, saw himself as Tatum's equal. That was especially true after Brown led the Celtics to 56 wins last season while Tatum missed the majority of the campaign rehabbing from a torn Achilles.

Trading Brown for George established a clear hierarchy in the locker room. The Celtics are Tatum's team, and George is happy to play a supporting role. Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla praised George for being "very coachable, very open-minded" and setting a "very high" standard.

"The way we're asking him to play is maybe a little bit different than what he's been asked to do in the past. He enjoys that, he's open-minded to it and he just works at it. He's very hard on himself. Holds himself to a very high standard, constantly watching film, taking notes in his journal and just processing the game. He takes pride in learning and getting better and you're seeing the fruits of that," Mazzulla said Sunday.

George has always been a high-level 3-point shooter, but he's spent most of his career having to create looks for himself. In Boston, playing alongside Tatum in a system that prioritizes shooting and spacing, George has thrived as a high-volume catch-and-shoot threat.

He's shooting 46% on 5.6 catch-and-shoot 3-point attempts per game -- both marks are career-highs. George is tied for 10th in the league in catch-and-shoot 3-point attempts per game, and among the 16 players taking at least five such attempts, he's tied for second in percentage, behind only Steph Curry (54.9%).

Most efficient high-volume catch-and-shoot threats in 2026-27

By comparison, Brown has never shot 40% from 3-point range for a season in his career, and hasn't even shot above 40% on catch-and-shoot attempts since 2021. George's willingness to accept more of an off-ball role, and ability to knock down those shots at an extremely high rate, is a big reason why he's fit in so seamlessly in Boston.

George's five 3s against the Bucks on Sunday were all of the catch-and-shoot variety.

"Watching him shoot like that is unbelievable," Celtics big man Mitchell Robinson said Sunday. "Played against him quite a few times and to be on the same side of the ball with him and cheer him on instead of boo[ing him], it's great."

Overall, George is shooting 42.5% on a team-high 8.1 3-point attempts per game. His hot shooting is a big reason why the Celtics are sixth in the league in 3-point percentage (37.6%) even though Tatum (31.3%) and Derrick White (32.7%) have been ice cold to start the season.

George hasn't made an All-Defensive Team since 2019, when he finished third in Defensive Player of the Year voting with the Oklahoma City Thunder, in large part due to injuries. He remains an elite team defender, though, and will get back to the All-Defensive level this season if he stays healthy and keeps defending like he has through the first 10 games.

When asked about George on Sunday, Tatum singled out his new teammate's "super-high IQ" and "incredible defensive instincts."

George has been particularly impressive off the ball this season. He's wreaking havoc in the passing lanes with his length, timing and anticipation. George's 2.3 steals are a career-high and good for fourth in the league, and he's third in deflections per game with 5.1. Of the four players averaging at least five deflections per game, he is by far the oldest at 36.

George's effort is a big reason why the Celtics are forcing way more turnovers than they ever have under Mazzulla. Their opponent turnover rate is 17.4%, which ranks sixth in the league; in Mazzulla's first four seasons in charge, the Celtics never had an opponent turnover rate above 13.1% and never finished higher than 24th in the league in that category.

#2639. MLB rumors: Why the Cubs may already be out on Tarik Skubal, plus latest on Phillies, Cardinals, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 2 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22.

Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace, offseason rumors are already flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Monday's supply just below.

The expectation remains that we'll see some level of activity on the trade and free agency fronts before the lockout begins in early December. As noted above, that was indeed the case leading up to the last lockout, and this time around, the prospect of drastic changes in the next CBA may have big-spending teams looking to fortify their rosters before those changes are implemented. Speaking of which, MLB Network reports that we could see some notable transactions go down at the upcoming General Managers Meetings, which take place from Nov. 10-12 in Las Vegas.

During a standard offseason, not much beyond behind-the-scenes groundwork goes down during the GM Meetings, and the real moves start happening at the December Winter Meetings. However, unless the lockout is resolved quickly – highly unlikely – then there probably won't be a Winter Meetings this offseason. That means the GM Meetings could be more active than usual.

Free agent ace and, until later this week, reigning back-to-back  American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal is the prize of the offseason. The 29-year-old lefty is a fit for any of MLB's 30 teams, but heretofore the most serious bidders have been expected to be the Los Angeles Dodgers (who acquired Skubal from the Detroit Tigers leading up to last season's trade deadline), the New York Mets, and the Chicago Cubs. Now, though, perhaps you can reduce that number of serious bidders to two. While Chicago very much needs rotation help for 2027 and beyond, the Athletic reports that the Cubs "are expected to stay on the sidelines" when the Skubal bidding gets serious. That, no doubt, will come as a disappointment to Cubs fans who are still waiting for the Ricketts to invest in the payroll at levels befitting a big-market contender.

The Cardinals traded away veteran lefty reliever JoJo Romero, along with starter and fellow free agent Dustin May, to the Milwaukee Brewers leading up to the trade deadline. Now, St. Louis may be interested in bringing Romero back on a free agent contract, the St. Louis Post-Dispatch reports.

Romero, 30, is coming off a 2026 season in which he pitched to a 3.36 ERA with a 3.00 K/BB ratio in 55 appearances. In the postseason with Milwaukee, Romero had a 1.13 ERA with 11 strikeouts and one walk in eight innings. He previously spent parts of five seasons with the Cardinals.

Do the Philadelphia Phillies need a new shortstop? That's one of the principal questions of their offseason. Although incumbent Trea Turner is signed through 2033, his defense at the crucial position of shortstop has degraded into "unplayable" territory, and that has the Phils considering fallback options should Turner need to be moved off the position. One option is free agent 31-year-old Ha-Seong Kim, NBC Sports Philadelphia reports. Kim, 32, spent last season on a one-year deal with the division-rival Atlanta Braves. He's been a primary shortstop for five of his six MLB seasons, and while he's certainly not among the very best at the position, he does profile as a major defensive upgrade over Turner. As for the bat, Kim for his career has an OPS+ of 93, and he's capable of stealing a base on occasion. He was, however, an offensive sinkhole for 51 games in 2026. Turner, meantime, may be looking at a switch to the outfield starting next season as the Phillies attempt to keep their contending window open.

#2638. Grading every NFL team at the midway point: Chargers get an 'F,' three teams get solid 'A' grade

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We're just past the midway point of the NFL season, which means it's time to start thinking seriously about who has and has not met the expectations we set for them at the start of the year. Everyone came into the season with a different set of hopes, and everyone has had plenty of time to meet, exceed or fall short of them now that we have played nine weeks of football.

For some teams, whether they have done what was expected of them is fairly obvious: The Chargers have not, for example. For other teams, it's not so obvious: The entire NFC South would fit that description. But what about the rest of the teams in the league? How have they performed, and how would we grade them relative to what was expected of them entering the season?

That's why we're here. We're assigning letter grades to each team's performance through the midway point of the season. We broke down where each team stands, and why, below.

Dallas came into this season with high hopes but has instead disappointed. The Cowboys' defense remains a disaster, and the offense hasn't lived up to expectations. They've also blown a couple of games with poor situational football awareness. The only thing saving them from a worse grade is that the rest of the NFC East is bad enough that they're in second place and potentially in position to make a run at the playoffs.

Notwithstanding their Thursday night loss to Washington, the Giants could hardly have hoped for the start of the John Harbaugh era to go any better results-wise. They're in first place in the division despite having lost their starting quarterback in the second game of the season. Rookie Arvell Reese looks like a total monster. They have mostly won close games, so they might not be as good as their record indicates, but that doesn't matter when it comes to how they've performed relative to expectations.

The Eagles would have an F if not for Howie Roseman's smart pivot to selling off pieces at and around the trade deadline, which restocked the cupboard full of draft picks for the future. Philly is always smart about knowing when to pull the plug on a lost season, which is exactly what this year has been.

The Commanders weren't necessarily expected to be all that competitive in the NFC East this year, but the degree to which they've fallen behind the Giants and Cowboys is disappointing. The game management issues under Dan Quinn have also persisted, which contributes to this grade.

The Bears, like the rest of the NFC North, have to be happy with how their season has gone to date. The offense looks explosive, and the defense looks better after the addition of Jeffery Simmons. The only thing holding them back from getting a straight 'A' here is the surprising lack of run game efficiency, though Kyle Monangai's absence has contributed to that.

The Lions have one of the most explosive offenses in the league, with Jahmyr Gibbs, Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams and Sam LaPorta combining with Jared Goff to light up scoreboards. The defense has even been playing better lately, albeit in light matchups. There have been some issues here and there (like the loss to the Panthers), but overall, things have gone quite well relative to expectations.

The Packers have to be thrilled with how their season has gone. Despite the absence of Micah Parsons, the defense has been excellent. Jordan Love is playing near an MVP level. Christian Watson and Matthew Golden look like superstars. The one thing holding them back from an 'A' is how they started the season, with a bad loss to Minnesota and the blowout against Atlanta. Otherwise, things have gone about as well as could be expected.

The Vikings' defense gets an A+++++, but the offense has been bad enough to knock the team down nearly a full letter grade despite Minnesota's 6-2 record. Here's hoping that Kirk Cousins can at least prop things up a bit for the rest of the season.

I can't justify giving any NFC South team anything other than a 'C' based on what they have done to date. They're all living down to relatively low expectations.

The Cardinals have actually been better than anybody expected. They have three wins, and they've played a couple of other close games mixed in there. They do have five double-digit losses, though, so it's hard to give them a grade in the 'B' range. Things will also likely get worse the rest of the way, given their injury issues. That said, getting a second-round pick back for Marvin Harrison Jr. looks like a good deal.

The Super Team expectations were probably always a bit too high, but the Rams haven't come close for a variety of reasons. Whether it's injuries, Matthew Stafford's regression or even more injuries, you have to dock the Rams for not even being a surefire playoff team at the midpoint of the season. Being over .500 despite the injuries is mildly impressive, but not enough to give them a grade in the 'B' range.

The 49ers are a team that has overcome nearly as many injuries as the Rams have faced. And Raheem Morris has the defense playing well despite its own injury issues. They've been great on both sides of the ball.

We initially had the Seahawks at a 'B-' grade, but then we remembered the odd loss to the Commanders in Week 3 and had to knock them down. Seattle has navigated some offseason losses (Klint Kubiak, Kenneth Walker III and more) and injury issues (the entire backfield), and three of its four losses came in one-score games, but we expected the Seahawks to be closer to the top of the division than they are right now.

The Bills have overcome a questionable defense to emerge midway through the season with a 7-1 record. Josh Allen is firmly in the MVP mix once again. James Cook is averaging even more rushing yards per game than he did a year ago. The offense has kept humming despite DJ Moore missing time. The Joe Brady era is off to a very good start.

The Dolphins have played right around expectations so far this year. They have smartly played at a snail's pace on offense to try and shorten games and stay competitive, which has resulted in them losing by less than expected in some contests, and they even beat the Jets. Still, it's hard to justify better than a 'C' grade when you're 1-7 at the halfway point.

The Patriots' start to the season was terrible. They then got on a little bit of a run to bounce back, and it looked like they might recapture some of what they had last year. But they've lost two games against good teams over the last three weeks, and they got smacked by the Packers in the most recent one. The injury issues on offense matter, but sitting at 5-4 before their trip to Munich is a slight disappointment.

The Jets look like they have a nice corps of young players on both offense and defense, but they're also 2-7. It's hard to find the appropriate grade for that type of team, especially when it's coming off its worst loss of the season, where it was totally non-competitive. It feels like a 'C+' is just right, relative to what we expected from them coming into this year.

Considering they haven't had Lamar Jackson for much of the season (he basically played 3.5 games), it's at least somewhat impressive that the Ravens are still in the mix in the AFC at 4-5. But they've lost four games in a row and have looked inept offensively of late (albeit in brutal situations), and Jesse Minter's defense hasn't been able to make up for it.

The Bengals' offense started the season somewhat slowly, as per usual, but has kicked into high gear of late, as per usual. Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins are basically unstoppable, and the defense is improved relative to recent years. There have been some ups and downs with that unit (27 points against the Bucs despite four turnovers, 30 against the Steelers, 24 against the Dolphins despite three turnovers, 36 against the Titans despite two turnovers), so that's keeping them from earning a straight 'A' here.

The Browns are 5-4, which would make you think they should get an 'A' relative to expectations. But when you look at the context of those games, and the fact that they each required a game-winning drive in the final five minutes, you see that the record isn't as impressive as it looks on the surface. Still, the wins count, and five is probably more than many people expected them to get coming into the year.

The inexcusable loss to the Browns back in Week 4 keeps the Steelers out of the 'A' range, which they might otherwise be in, given their offense and defense. The run game has been impressive, and the defense has maintained a high level of play. Coming out of their bye at 6-2 is an ideal midseason result.

The Texans are 3-5, and two of their wins have come against the Titans and Chargers. Their defense has regressed year over year. That all overshadows the great season they're getting out of C.J. Stroud, who has been even better this year than he was during his spectacular rookie season.

The Colts have been a disaster on both sides of the ball and had to enter fire-sale mode. This grade would be lower if not for the fact that they did get some assets for a few players who were obviously on their way out the door.

The Jaguars are 6-2 with two one-score losses, and they look elite on both offense and defense. They might have an inside track on the No. 1 seed in the AFC, given their rest-of-season strength of schedule. We docked them to an 'A-' thanks only to the frankly bonkers price they paid in the Jordan Davis trade, even if he is going to help their defense the rest of the way.

The Titans looked more competent in their final three games going into their Week 9 bye, even if they did lose two of them. The offense looked so bad early in the year, though, that we can't even justify giving them a straight 'C' here. We're grading the entire season to date, not just what's happened most recently. Getting a second-round pick and more for Amani Hooker was nice, though.

I don't know how the Broncos keep getting away with it in one-score games (6-0 this season), but they do. They're probably not as good as their 6-2 record suggests, and they got embarrassed in the season opener against Kansas City, but there's no denying their track record of winning in clutch situations at this point. So, we're giving them a bit of credit for it here.

The Chiefs have taken care of business for the most part this season, losing only to the Seahawks and Broncos on the road in back-to-back weeks. They have otherwise been able to run the ball at will on everyone, and their defense has been excellent. The blip in Weeks 7 and 8 counts, though, and it revealed an inability to find a way to win if Kenneth Walker doesn't go off. That matters.

Things worked out quite nicely for the Raiders. They started out 3-0, Kirk Cousins played well enough to give Fernando Mendoza time to sit and learn for half a season, and then they got a third-round pick for Cousins at the deadline. If they hadn't lost five of their last six games, this grade would be even higher.

#2636. Miami Heat to host 2028 NBA All-Star Weekend, first time since 1990, per report

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Miami is one of the sports world's most beloved event hosts. Super Bowls and National Championship Games are frequently held in South Florida, but for quite some time, the NBA's marquee regular-season event has been held elsewhere. The Miami Heat hosted All-Star Weekend in 1990, their second season in existence, but haven't hosted it since.

Well, that's about to change. Miami will host the event in 2028, after Phoenix does so in 2027, according to ESPN. The decision comes on the heels of widespread complaints about All-Star Weekends being held in smaller, less desirable cities to visit.

In 2024, The Oklahoman, questioning why Oklahoma City was not hosting the event, reported that the NBA planned to start enforcing minimums on certain amenities for prospective All-Star markets, including at least 7,250 hotel rooms and three five-star hotels, at least 650,000 square feet of convention center and exhibition space, and at least 75 nonstop domestic flights and at least 20 international flights. The NBA denied that these were ironclad requirements. Miami is the second city to earn an All-Star Weekend since that report, joining Phoenix, as San Francisco (2025) and Los Angeles (2026) were already settled. All four cities are notably relatively warm in February.

So, why did it take so long for Miami in particular to get a second All-Star Weekend? The answer may be the Miami International Boat Show, which occupies much of the city's hotel and convention space capacity and usually comes during Presidents' Day weekend, which often conflicts with the NBA's All-Star schedule. However, the Boat Show will reportedly be moving to a different weekend in 2028 to accommodate the NBA, which will hold All-Star Weekend from Feb. 18-20.

The Heat did not put in a bid to host All-Star Weekend, according to the Miami Herald, and have typically avoided doing so in the past. Instead, the NBA reportedly approached the Heat about hosting, and now, Miami will get its first All-Star Game in almost four decades.

#2633. Predicting 2027 MLB Rookie of the Year candidates: Josue De Paula, Kade Anderson, Jesús Made and more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Tigers infielder Kevin McGonigle and Reds slugger Sal Stewart were named the 2026 Rookies of the Year on Monday night. McGonigle was the wire-to-wire leader for the award despite a stacked American League rookie class. In the National League, Stewart edged out Mets outfielder Carson Benge and Cardinals second baseman JJ Wetherholt, both of whom had excellent rookie campaigns.

No award gets you excited about the future the way Rookie of the Year does. It's a young player being recognized for his greatness, and great young players are what sports hopes are built on. With that in mind, here's a look ahead at the 2027 rookie class and, more importantly, who could be in the running for the 2027 Rookie of the Year awards.

Anderson made his debut in late August and gave the Mariners seven solid starts, though he remains rookie-eligible because he did not exceed the rookie limits of 50 innings or 45 days of service time. Anderson, the No. 3 pick in the 2025 Draft, is arguably the best pitching prospect in the game and is likely to have a rotation spot on Opening Day, which figures to boost his Rookie of the Year case. Add in a pitcher-friendly home ballpark, and Anderson is the super early favorite for the award. He had 167 strikeouts against only 22 walks in 129 innings between MLB and the minors in 2026.

One of the best prospects in the minors, Arias nearly made his MLB debut in September, but the Red Sox opted against it. He authored a .323/.400/.557 line with 25 home runs between Double-A and Triple-A in 2026, including a .331/.388/.506 line in 42 games at Triple-A as a 20-year-old. Trevor Story is entering the final year of his contract and has been healthy and productive at the same time once in the last four years. Arias likely gives Boston a better chance to win right now and I would not be surprised to see them turn the shortstop reins over to the youngster early next season. Early as in April.

Like Anderson, Jenkins made his MLB debut in late August, yet his rookie eligibility remains intact going into 2027. He had a rough go of it in the majors, slashing .226/.293/.393 in 26 games with the Twins, though his contact rates and plate discipline were impressive. Jenkins will turn only 22 in February and he is not the first top prospect to have a rough 26 games to begin his big-league career, nor will he be the last. There might be more growing pains to come next season, but Minnesota figures to give Jenkins a long runway to work through them. His 2027 could look like Benge's 2026, meaning sluggish early and sensational late.

It was only 11 games (plus four pinch-hitting appearances in the postseason), but gosh, De Paula was so impressive during his big-league debut. He's a precocious hitter with tremendous strike zone knowledge (13 walks and five strikeouts), and also some serious hard-hit ability. The biggest obstacle standing between De Paula and next year's Rookie of the Year award is playing time. Shohei Ohtani is locked in at DH and Andy Pages and Kyle Tucker aren't going anywhere. The Dodgers will have to either trade or bench Teoscar Hernández to get De Paula into the lineup. It would be worth it. The Yordan Alvarez comps De Paula got in the minors don't seem so insane now.

The Brewers are the World Series champions and they also have arguably the best farm system in the game with the consensus No. 1 prospect in Made. Still only 19, Made performed admirably in a full season at Double-A this year, and he's currently playing very well against grown men in the Dominican Winter League. He figures to open next season in Triple-A, with a May or June promotion to Milwaukee in the cards. That could put Made at a disadvantage in the Rookie of the Year race. Either way, it's only a matter of time until the defending champions add the game's best prospect to their lineup, presumably at third base.

At 20 years and 121 days, Salas became the youngest catcher to ever appear in a postseason game in Game 2 of this year's Wild Card Series. He started three of San Diego's six postseason games after making his MLB debut in September, and it seems likely Salas will take over as their starting backstop next season. I think he's a longshot Rookie of the Year candidate simply because it's really hard to be a rookie catcher, and next year Salas will be the youngest regular catcher since Hall of Famer Ivan Rodriguez in 1991. Still, Salas is a special defender with promising offensive chops.

Several prominent Japanese veterans will make their way to MLB via the posting system this offseason. We don't know where they will sign yet, but the rules say these players will be Rookie of the Year-eligible regardless of their age or years of experience in Japan, so we're going to include them here.

We ranked Sato as the best position player free agent on the market this offseason. Japan's reigning Triple Crown winner has tremendous left-handed power. We're talking legitimate 30-homer upside. Sato does swing and miss a bunch, though, and he's an aggressive hitter who's unlikely to walk as much as Munetaka Murakami, which could hold him back at the plate. Add in questionable defense at the hot corner and it's unclear exactly how much impact Sato will have in the big leagues. Bottom line though, guys with 30-homer power will always be in the Rookie of the Year conversation.

Taira, our No. 19 free agent, is destined to be a fan favorite given his fire hydrant build (5-foot-8 and 220 lbs.) and bat-missing fastball. He gets close to seven feet of extension down the mound despite his height, creating a unique release window and an "upshoot" effect on his fastball. Taira started for the Seibu Lions in 2026 after spending 2024 and 2025 in the bullpen. I assume the team that signs him will give him a chance to start next year. If he winds up in relief, Taira has the stuff and gumption to get high-leverage outs in the late innings.

#2632. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2631. Champions Classic NBA Draft guide: Who scouts will be watching in college basketball's high-profile showcase

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The most anticipated double-header of the young college basketball season takes place tonight in Chicago as No. 2 Duke meets No. 5 Michigan State, followed by No. 15 Kansas vs. No. 24 Kentucky in the Champions Classic.

The event is also expected to draw a heavy dose of NBA scouts and decision-makers to Chicago, given the opportunity to see so many high-level prospects under one roof on one night.

One wrinkle: The best NBA prospect on the court Tuesday night won't even be eligible to be drafted in 2027. That's Duke freshman Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje who is 17 years old and won't turn 18 until next May. In order to be eligible for the NBA Draft, a player must be at least 19 years old during the calendar year of the draft, per NBA rules.

So not only will Boumtje Boumtje be ineligible for the upcoming draft; he is expected back at Duke for his sophomore season.

Another thing to keep in mind is that these NBA scouts and executives will use what they see on Tuesday night as a benchmark and something to measure against for the rest of the season. They will not over-index on what they see on just one given night.

The public, on the other hand, has a tendency to fall for that trap. Because tonight is so visible, if someone has a glaring performance (good or bad), it often anchors a lot of the public discourse for the rest of the season. Trevor Keels is the classic example. He scored 25 points in the 2021 Champions Classic, was mocked as a lottery pick almost immediately afterwards, ended up declaring for the draft prematurely, and slipped to the second round.

The moral of the story – keep what you see on Tuesday night in perspective, because the people who make the big decisions certainly will.

So with all that in mind, here's a look at the top NBA prospects from the four teams in action at the Champions Classic

This shouldn't come as a surprise, but the Blue Devils lead the way in terms of total NBA prospects. What's interesting about this year's team though, is that their best prospect, Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje, isn't even eligible this year, but is the early favorite to be the top pick in 2028. Boumtje Boumtje has a combination of size and skill, which is unmatched for his age, not just in college basketball, but anywhere in the world.

Ngongba had a chance to be a first-round pick a year ago, but opted to return to Duke, and so far, it looks a decision that is going to pay off. Ngonba fits a coveted NBA archetype in that he's a mismatch five-man who can play inside and out. He is a vertical spacer, reliable passer, and consistent offensive rebounder who has massive length to also be a rim protector. Scouts want to see him take the next step as a shot-blocker and as a rebounder while proving his durability.

If Ngongba can prove he can space the floor with his shooting, that's just an added bonus. He's prepared for that challenge by getting himself into the best shape of his career and looks poised to be the focal point for the Blue Devils, at least on the interior, this season. In short, it's early, but the lottery is very much in play here.

Sarr is a long and athletic big wing who, last year as a freshman, was already one of the best perimeter defenders in the ACC, if not the country. This year, he's going to get the volume to show his offensive growth. So far, that's come more in transition and as a secondary playmaker, but what the NBA is going to be most interested in is his ability to make spot-up 3s in order to fit that coveted 3-and-D archetype. Sarr was 32% from that range last season, but hasn't even attempted a three through two games this year, but has gotten to the free-throw line in high volume and made 71%, after connecting on only 53% last year.

While the progression of Sarr's total game is important, scouts will be monitoring the shooting most closely all year long. Duke also appears to be recruiting as if they expect Sarr to move on after the year. The first-round should be the expectation, with the late lottery not being out of the question.

Williams has quickly become one of the most polarizing draft prospects in the country. He was a top five recruit out of the high school ranks a year ago because of his combination of size, athleticism, fluidity, skill, and shot-blocking potential, even with real questions about his physicality.

Williams has played a limited role to start the season and could fall further out of the rotation as games get closer. Nevertheless, it wouldn't be at all surprising to see him explore professional opportunities, even if this season doesn't go as expected. It also wouldn't be unprecedented to see a team invest a first-round pick in trying to develop his tools, even in that scenario. It's a trajectory that could mirror that of Peyton Watson, who was a prized 2021 recruit who didn't play much in his freshman season at UCLA, still declared for the draft, and ended up being the 30th pick for the Nuggets a year later. That pick has gone down as a very good one.

If the exhibition slate was any indication, Blackwell may be Duke's most reliable player this season. He came to Durham after putting up 19 points and 5 rebounds on 43/39/86 shooting last year for Wisconsin, but did not get any first-round traction in the pre-draft process.

The narrative once Blackwell hit the portal was that he wanted to play with the ball in his hands. Fortunately, he seems to have gotten over that, because his path to the NBA is based on proving he can be a reliable two-way role player, not an alpha creator. Duke is the biggest stage to prove that. If the shooting splits hold up and he can provide some secondary playmaking and be a defensive asset, then hopefully scouts won't be so worried about his lack of length come the next draft cycle.

NBA scouts are also watching: Deron Rippey Jr., 6-1, freshman, guard; Bryson Howard, 6-4, freshman, guard; Caleb Foster, 6-4, senior, guard; Cayden Boozer, 6-3, sophomore, guard.

The Spartans are unlike many of college basketball's other top programs in that while they are projected to be among the very best teams in the sport, but they don't have as many glaring NBA prospects. Of course, similar claims used to be made about Villanova teams of old, and that proved to be beyond shortsighted, so it's possible that time will prove the masses wrong about the individual talent on this year's team.

Fears is undoubtedly one of the best players and floor generals in all of college basketball. Everything Michigan State does begins with him, and the same was true last year for a team that won 27 games and advanced to the Sweet 16 before running into UConn. There are, however, questions about how his game translates to the NBA. He lacks ideal measurables for the league, doesn't have the outlier burst to compensate, and is also a questionable shooter.

Still, it's hard to bet against Fears' will, and so chances are he figures out how to stick at the next level. The elephant in the room, though, is that while he is a true senior this year at Michigan State, his earning potential will almost certainly be higher in college than the pros next year. The Spartans have recruited as if he's not going to be back, but if and when financial reality hits, will they be willing to tolerate seeing him in another uniform? Only time will tell.

The baby-faced sophomore is still a work in progress and just starting to grow into his body and fill out his frame. Right now, he is much more of a Robin to Fears' Batman for the Spartans. And yet, Scott has a game that could ultimately translate to the next level more seamlessly. He's a big wing with positional size, a reliable floor-spacer who made 37% of his threes last year as a freshman. He's also a reliable decision-maker who turned the ball over a total of 32 times in 729 minutes a year ago. In short, the NBA is intrigued, so whether or not it's this year or down the road, Scott is on the right trajectory.

NBA scouts are also watching: Coen Carr, 6-6, senior, forward; Jasiah Jervis, 6-4, freshman, guard; Ethan Taylor, 7-2, freshman, center.

For the second consecutive year, Bill Self has a freshman with a chance to prove he should be the top pick in the draft. The biggest question for most of the summer, though, was based on who else they could get to surround Tyran Stokes. Now, thanks to eligibility being granted to Melvin Council, Tre White, and Tre Kaufman-Renn, the Jayhawks suddenly have an ideal supporting cast. Here's the thing, though: if those guys were NBA players at this point, they wouldn't have been available to return.

Stokes is the early favorite to be the top pick in the 2027 NBA draft. He's built like a throwback power forward, but can initiate like a guard, not just for himself, but for others as well. The biggest questions in high school were about his approach and ability to impact winning on a daily basis, but so far at Kansas, he's gotten rave reviews. Being surrounded by veterans no doubt helps, as does having some reinforcements. When Stokes dropped 27 points, eight rebounds, and seven assists on Duke in an exhibition, it was a sign of things to come. That performance came without the Jayhawks having yet established an ideal scheme to get him going in space and movement. In short, if Stokes' mindset stays the same, he has a chance to distance himself from the field this season, and that process could begin tonight.

NBA scouts are also watching: Taylen Kinney, 6-2, freshman, guard; Keanu Dawes, 6-9, senior, forward; Melvin Council Jr, 6-4, graduate, guard; Tre White, 6-6, graduate, wing; Trey Kaufman-Renn, 6-8, graduate, center/forward.

Malachi Moreno and Milan Momcilovic both had a good chance to be drafted last June. So, when they opted to return, it wasn't for a lack of options; it was for the valuation that college basketball, and Kentucky in particular, was able to pay them. That's a very different calculus than graduate students who return after not signing NBA contracts. So, while this year's roster may not have any glaring lottery picks, it does have pro talent.

Moreno fits a coveted archetype in today's NBA because he has legit size and can be reliable in offensive structure. He's a quick processor of the game and a reliable decision-maker at various spots on the floor. He's a solid passer, efficient finisher, and may even have some long-term shooting potential. He also provides some defensive rim protection, but could certainly help his stock this season by becoming more assertive around the rim on both ends of the floor. The first-round should be the goal for Moreno coming out of this season.

Momcilovic was one of the best shooters in college basketball last year, making 49% of his threes on almost 8 attempts per game, while also making 88% of his free throws for good measure. Through two games at Kentucky, he's getting even more volume, with 17 attempted threes in just two games so far. While his floor-spacing gravity is not in doubt, the questions for the next level are more about his ability to defend his position without putting his team in rotation. So, all-year scouts will be locked in on some of the nuances of Momcilovic's game, like his foot speed, angles, and rotations. Long-term, Momcilovic has positional size and a translatable niche, but may be in a familiar spot in the off-season, with more guaranteed money in the college ranks.

Wilkins was one of the best mid-major freshmen in the country last year, posting nearly 18 points and 5 assists for a Furman that went to the NCAA Tournament. He's a classic late-bloomer who had an undeveloped, wiry frame in high school, but quickly started to put things together as he grew into his body.

While he's still filling out, Wilkins is naturally smooth with real playmaking genes. Through two games at Kentucky, there's also been an early uptick in his shooting (he's 5-for-11 from three and 6-for-6 from the free-throw line). If that growth is sustainable, he'll continue to build momentum with NBA decision-makers. Exactly what his timeline will be, though, still remains to be seen.

NBA scouts are also watching: Kam Williams, 6-7, junior, wing; Zoom Diallo, 6-5, junior, guard; Mason Williams, 6-2, freshman, guard

#2630. 2026 MLB Rookie of the Year: Tigers' Kevin McGonigle, Reds' Sal Stewart win BBWAA awards

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Kevin McGonigle of the Tigers and Sal Stewart of the Reds were named the 2026 Rookies of the Year in their respective leagues on Monday night as part of the BBWAA's awards week. McGonigle earned 28 of 30 first-place votes, beating out the Guardians' Parker Messick and the Red Sox's Payton Tolle. Stewart, meanwhile, beat the Mets' Carson Benge and the Cardinals' JJ Wetherholt.

Because McGonigle and Stewart were both with the major-league team for long enough to earn a full year of service time, the Tigers and Reds will each receive a Prospect Promotion Incentive pick in the 2027 MLB Draft.

The annual awards, which also include Manager of the Year, Reliever of the Year, Cy Young and MVP, are voted on by 30 members of the Baseball Writers Association of America (that's two per MLB city in each league). Votes were submitted before the beginning of the playoffs, meaning that only regular-season contributions are taken into account.

Stewart won the battle of Old School stats vs. New School stats here. Though he only posted 2.0 WAR, he had 32 home runs and 111 RBI, putting him in rarefied air for a rookie. He's one of just 15 rookies ever with at least 30 homers and 100 RBI. The only names from that list to not win the award either faced another player from the list or played before Rookie of the Year was awarded. Everyone else has taken home the hardware, just as Stewart did Monday evening.

Overall, Stewart appeared in all 162 games, hitting .263/.330/.457 (117 OPS+) with 25 doubles, 32 homers, 112 RBI, 87 runs and 15 steals.

Stewart earned 20 of the 30 available first-place votes.

Carson Benge of the Mets finished second and JJ Wetherholt of the Cardinals finished in third place. Benge, the 2024 first-rounder, made the team out of spring training and hit .282/.346/.430 with 20 home runs, 22 steals and 4.3 WAR. Defensive metrics love Wetherholt and helped push him to 4.5 WAR in 139 games. He hit .242/.339/.365 with 17 homers, 14 steals and 89 runs.

Stewart joins the following Reds as Rookie of the Year winners:

The honor for McGonigle completes a stellar year for the former first-round draft pick. He broke camp with the Tigers and was productive from the get-go. He ended up hitting .278/.376/.430 (126 OPS+) with 28 doubles, five triples, 18 home runs, 72 RBI, 97 runs, 12 steals and 7.1 WAR, the latter good enough for the AL lead among position players. He played great defense, ran the bases well and was an All-Star. He nearly walked (95) as much as he struck out (100), too. Not much more could've been asked of the Pennsylvania native who played most of the season at age 21, and he's a well-deserving Rookie of the Year.

A few weeks after he debuted, he and the team agreed to an eight-year, $150 million extension.

McGonigle won in a blowout, getting 28 of the 30 available first-place votes, scoring 204 of a possible 210 points.

He joins the following players who have won the award with the Tigers:

Parker Messick of the Guardians finishes second after going 12-9 with a 2.56 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 193 strikeouts in 186 ⅓ innings; he is also a top-three finalist for the Cy Young award. Red Sox starter Payton Tolle finishes third after going 9-6 with a 3.03 ERA (135 ERA+), 1.10 WHIP and 171 strikeouts in 148 ⅔ innings.

#2629. One fatal flaw of every Super Bowl contender from 49ers depth to Packers run game

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Normally, when I write, I deal in optimism. Giving fans a reason for hope, something to look forward to when their favorite team takes the field.

The NFL trade deadline has come and gone, and while most teams have improved their chances at winning a Super Bowl, I'm here to pour a little bit of cold water on the excitement. No team is perfect, especially this year, when it feels like there's much more parity across the board. While there are obvious Super Bowl contenders, even those teams have flaws that could stop them from hoisting the Lombardi Trophy come February. Let's break down the fatal flaw of every contender at midseason, and if it comes true, then you can blame me.

*Contenders chosen using DraftKings Sportsbook midseason Super Bowl odds

I'm convinced the 49ers are living their own separate version of the movie "Groundhog Day." Every year they come in as legitimate contenders, then it all unravels because of injury. Well, this year is no different, with their depth already being tested.

On the defensive side of the ball, standout rookie DT Gracen Halton is going to miss the rest of the season with a broken ankle, and CBs Deommodore Lenoir and Renardo Green are both nursing foot injuries (but those are more day-to-day, according to Kyle Shanahan). Offensively, WR Mike Evans hasn't played since week 6, and WR Deebo Samuel hasn't played since week 5. They've gotten by with playing WRs Jordan Watkins, Brandin Cooks and Demarcus Robinson , but that's not a Super Bowl-winning trio. However, they did recently trade for Keenan Allen.

The spin zone here is that the cavalry is coming for reinforcements. Adding DT DeForest Buckner before the trade deadline was a huge move for the defensive line, helping them get more pressure without blitzing (the 49ers are 30th in the NFL in blitz rate and 20th in sack rate without blitzing). I've been a fan of what DC Raheem Morris has been able to get out of this defense, playing to the speed at the second and third level, and adding Buckner to that group should let the secondary play even faster (losing Halton sucks, though).

The more worrisome part is Evans, who is still more than likely not going to play against Dallas next week. Achilles tendinitis is scary, especially at Evans' age. He was such a critical part of why the Niners offense was back to the face-melting unit they've been in previous years, and if he can't go for the long haul, I worry about how this team can win the Super Bowl.

Despite adding safety Amani Hooker at the trade deadline, I still think the Bills' pass defense overall is the weakest part of the unit. As long as they don't get to play Carson Wentz every week, the Bills' pass defense is going to be what holds them back.

The Bills' defensive line has been a revelation this season; with the growth of EDGE Greg Rousseau and DT Deone Walker, the Bills are eighth in the NFL in pressure rate. However, their splits when they're under pressure versus when they're not are staggering. According to TruMedia, when they get pressure, they have a 69.5% defensive success rate and 0.15 defensive EPA/dropback. Combine all plays where they force a PBU, INT, TFL and sack together when they get pressure, and you get a 21.9% havoc rate when recording a pressure. When they don't get pressure, their defensive success rate drops to 45.5% (only above the Raiders), -0.31 defensive EPA per dropback, and that havoc rate? Yeah, it drops to 11.4%. Not a great look for their coverage unit.

The biggest problem is that they give up explosive plays, and while some of that should be ironed out by adding Hooker, I worry that DC Jim Leonhard just doesn't have the guys to prevent explosive plays in the middle of the field. If you just whittle it down to passing attempts between the hashmarks in the middle of the field, they've given up the second most completions of 20 or more yards in that area in the NFL. If they can't limit big plays, I worry about how much will be on the offense to keep cleaning up the defense's mistakes.

The Jacksonville Jaguars have arrived. After starting the season 6-2, the Jaguars made a massive splash at the trade deadline, acquiring S Jessie Bates and DT Jordan Davis to shore up two of their bigger issues on the defensive line. However, if this team falls before winning a Super Bowl, it'll be because of their pass protection.

On the surface, the Jaguars' offensive line looks good. They're tied for the fifth-lowest sacks allowed this season and eighth-lowest pressure rate allowed. On top of that, the Jaguars' ability to grind games down by running the football has been evident this season. However, digging into those numbers and watching the Jaguars play tells a different story.

In the passing game, Trevor Lawrence has been incredible this season at mitigating pressure and getting the ball out (a major part of his MVP case). Then, in the run game, the Jaguars are only above the Raiders in average yards before contact per carry, at 0.68 (their yards after contact per carry are 3.40, 6th in the NFL). The offensive line has been overwhelmed by interior pressure, with rookie LG Emmanuel Pregnon and RG Ezra Cleveland up and down in pass protection. Starting LT Anton Harrison has been lost for the season, and while Walker Little has performed admirably in his absence, it'll always be a worry for the Jaguars.

Lawrence has, like I said, been amazing at mitigating pressure and making plays around it. But in order to get out of the AFC, they'll have to face guys like Zach Allen, Dexter Lawrence, Cameron Heyward and more. If this team doesn't get to the Super Bowl, it'll be because the offensive line fell apart.

The Bears and the Jaguars back-to-back in Super Bowl contender stories — what a beautiful world we live in. The Bears look like one of the most complete teams in the NFL, with an offense that can score at will or grind teams into dust. To complement that offense, the Bears added a nitro boost to the defense by trading for DT Jeffrey Simmons, and that trade already looks like it paid off. However, if this team doesn't win the whole thing this year, it'll be because of a secondary that has been…volatile to say the least.

This isn't to say the Bears' secondary isn't talented. Kyler Gordon is an awesome nickel, and I've been impressed with the play of rookie Malik Muhammad on the outside. However, Muhammad has missed the last two games with a toe injury, leaving the Bears thin in the secondary. The mainstay of the group, CB Jaylon Johnson, has been inconsistent this season as well. I was of the belief that the Bears should've added another corner at the deadline to just give them some more insurance, but by not adding anyone, it shows a lot of belief in that group. I wouldn't believe in that group as much, and if they don't win it all, it'll be because the secondary fell apart.

I never thought I'd say this about a Patrick Mahomes-led unit, but the Chiefs' passing game isn't very explosive. Kansas City is only 21st in the NFL in completions of 20 or more yards this season, despite having a high rate of explosive passes. That is probably because only 14.4% of Patrick Mahomes' passing attempts this season are between 11 and 20 air yards, and only 8.4% are over 20 air yards, both near the bottom of the NFL.

Without WR Tyquan Thornton on the field, there's nobody who can win on passes downfield. Among all the Chiefs receivers this season, Thornton still leads the team in receptions of at least 16 or more air yards, despite going down in Week 4. Xavier Worthy leads the team in targets in that metric, but he only has two catches at that range. Not being able to hit any explosives makes the offense so much more congested, leaving the run game too little space to breathe and allowing opposing defenses to squat on all the crossing routes Kansas City likes to run.

The Chiefs did add a receiver at the deadline, trading for Indy's Josh Downs. Where Downs will help is in creating separation against man coverage and loosening up the offense in the intermediate game so Rice can be the over-the-top and YAC guy. But this team is still missing that third gear downfield. Worthy hasn't been consistent and is now out with a hamstring injury, so adding someone with size and speed in free agency could be key (Darius Slayton could be fun).

Maybe the hope is that the run game provides the explosives, which is definitely possible. But if the Chiefs fail to win the Super Bowl for the third straight year, it'll be because they can't create any explosive passes.

This Bengals team feels like a warm hug, a truly vintage Burrow-era Bengals unit. One of the most face-melting offenses the NFL has seen (doing it without even wanting to run the ball or getting under center), and a field-tilting defensive lineman who can absolutely take over. However, if this team isn't raising the Lombardi at the end of the season, it'll be because of some real shoddy linebacker play.

The trio of Barrett Carter, Demetrius Knight Jr and Oren Burks doesn't exactly inspire confidence, especially when it comes to pass coverage. All three guys are better at flowing fast downhill and creating negative plays in the run game, but their eyes can be manipulated in coverage. The Bengals are tied for the fifth-most plays of over 20 yards allowed on play action in the NFL this season, and in both of their losses, the Bengals linebackers have been poor in coverage. Because they are fitting the run so aggressively, they leave themselves susceptible to explosives in the middle of the field off play action, which is where every team is trying to hunt in the NFL.

If you look at all the teams in the AFC, they're all incredible at manipulating linebackers via play action and getting wires crossed. For the Bengals to beat teams like Buffalo, Jacksonville, Kansas City and Pittsburgh, their linebacker play needs to improve in pass coverage. I'm a little surprised they didn't try to add to the linebacker room at the trade deadline, but given how their first trade went down, it makes sense they bowed out after that. Either way, their linebacker play hasn't been up to par this season, and it could be their downfall.

If I had a nickel for every time an NFL "Superteam" was unraveled by injury and poor play, I'd have two nickels. That's not a lot, but the fact that it happened twice is relevant. The Rams have gone from being everyone's Super Bowl favorite to being on the brink of missing the playoffs entirely, a cataclysmic drop that will have many people asking what happened.

Aside from the obvious caveat that everyone important on the team has been hurt at some point this season, I think the biggest reason this team hasn't been the same unit is that they can't hit explosive passes. Take this as a comparison: According to TruMedia, the Rams had a 15.9% explosive pass rate last season, good for sixth in the NFL. In 2026, that number has dropped to 10.8%, below teams like the Miami Dolphins and Pittsburgh Steelers.

Now, part of that has legitimately been due to injuries to players like WR Davante Adams, TE Terrance Ferguson and now WR Puka Nacua, but Matthew Stafford just hasn't been accurate outside the numbers this season. A large part of their explosive offense last year was Stafford catching fire on those passes, drilling corners and out routes to stop defenses from congesting the middle of the field.

Overall, TruMedia has Stafford's off-target rate jumping up three percentage points this season, but when you specify passes on the sideline or outside the numbers, his off-target rate has jumped from 15% in 2025 to 28.6% this season. That's an alarming uptick in inaccuracy, one that is telling for an older QB like Stafford. If he can't drill those passes, the offense becomes much more difficult. If the Rams want to make the playoffs, they need to get healthy. If they want to win a Super Bowl, Stafford has to hit those passes more often.

As it currently stands, the Broncos have a 37.1% passing success rate, 28th in the NFL. Since 2010, the worst passing offense to win a Super Bowl by that metric is the 2015 Denver Broncos…who were at 42.2%. It would be historically unprecedented for a team with as bad a passing offense as the Broncos to win the Super Bowl, and it's by far the Broncos' biggest flaw.

Now, I will add that every year the Broncos' passing game starts off slow and then picks up by the time the playoffs roll around, and so far this season that's proven to be the case. However, I still think the passing offense is far too inconsistent for me to trust them in close game scenarios.

For the Broncos to win the Super Bowl, Nix has to consistently hit the designed passes in the middle of the field. He's done a better job of that recently than in previous weeks, but against healthy secondaries I worry that the offense will turtle back on itself and not allow Sean Payton's well-designed offense to click. Everything is in position for this offense to once again hit their late-season surge, but if they want to win a Super Bowl, the passing game needs to start clicking.

Everyone is wondering what's wrong with the Seahawks' offense this season. Is it a decline from QB Sam Darnold? OC Brian Fleury doesn't pull the same levers as Klint Kubiak did? Is it just general regression? In a way, all of these are correct, but the root of the problem is that they aren't an explosive running team this season.

Last year, while the Seahawks' run game wasn't "great" (-0.04 EPA per carry, 39.5% rushing success rate on all designed runs), they had a 7.3% explosive rushing rate. This season, the Seahawks' run game has fallen off a cliff, putting up a putrid -0.20 EPA per carry, 33.5% rushing success rate and a 6.2% explosive rushing rate. Even last season when the Seahawks' run game wasn't exactly the most efficient, you could count on at least a few explosive runs from their offense to keep the thought in defenses' heads and make the game easier on Darnold. Without any explosive runs AND being inefficient, the Seahawks consistently put themselves behind the sticks and in obvious passing situations, where Darnold doesn't thrive.

There is a solution to this problem: Quenton Nelson. The Seahawks traded for the LG before the deadline, and he looked as advertised before going down with an injury. Once he and LT Charles Cross get back, the run game could improve. But if the Seahawks fail to repeat, you can blame the lack of explosive runs.

Remember earlier when I said the Bills have a problem preventing explosive plays? Ditto for the Lions, who have been hit by the injury bug once again. Despite getting S Brian Branch back, the secondary still has issues with defending the pass.

Per Sumer Sports, the Lions are 22nd in the NFL in passing success rate allowed and 28th in EPA/pass allowed. The biggest issue has come when they play man coverage, leaving their cornerbacks on islands. CB DJ Reed has made the occasional big play, but CB Rock Ya-Sin has been targeted often, as has Roger McCreary. The back-end coverage play has undone what has been a very good season for their defensive front, preventing them from getting home and making plays.

The Lions' offense is Super Bowl caliber, and I think their defensive line can play up to that level as well. But the depth on this team continues to be tested, and now without LB Jack Campbell and S Kerby Joseph, getting by in the secondary will just have to do.

I'm not joking when I say the Packers' rushing offense is one of the worst units in football this year. Through nine games, the only three teams worse than Green Bay on the ground based on rushing success rate are the Miami Dolphins, Las Vegas Raiders and Cleveland Browns (per TruMedia). If we use EPA per rush, the Packers are dead last.

Now there are multiple symptoms for this, and they're all bad. The offensive line can't get enough push to run the gap scheme runs the Packers want to get into (29th in yards before contact per carry), and the Packers' RBs have also given the team next to nothing when it comes to making people miss. As a team, the Packers are 30th in yards after contact per carry and 27th in percentage of tackles avoided.

The offensive line has been unsettled since losing RT Zach Bako-Bewele to injury, and because they haven't had a chance to find their best five, the run game has been awful. Combine that with the running back room not having any form of juice, and you get needing WR Savion Williams to be your best threat running the football.

With QB Jordan Love and the defense playing as well as they are right now, it should be easy to call the Packers a Super Bowl team. But if they don't make it there, it'll be because they can't run the football and make it easier on themselves.

Since 2000, there have been 379 teams with winning records through nine games. The 2026 Minnesota Vikings rank 379th in offensive success rate.

We could end this right there, but let's dig into why every time the Vikings offense takes the field, it feels like a win for the other team. First of all, the accuracy of any QB under center has been erratic. This season, among QBs with at least 50 dropbacks, both Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz are in the top 10 in off-target rate per TruMedia. The Minnesota offense doesn't have a lot of built-in easy buttons for throwing the football; much of it is about attacking vertically and pushing the ball to hunt explosives. So when these plays are missing, you dig yourself into a lot of second/third and longs.

You can offset this by using your run game, always staying ahead of the sticks and freeing your QB to take downfield shots because you know you can get 4-5 yards on the ground. Well, the Vikings sit at 29th in rushing success rate and average the second-lowest yards after contact per carry in the NFL. So if you're not accurate and you can't run the ball either, you get an easy recipe for one of the worst offenses the NFL has ever seen (no exaggeration!)

Here are the worst NFL offenses since 2010 based on Offensive Success Rate in general, through weeks 1-9.The Minnesota Vikings are 6-2 https://t.co/DBiFNooUNh pic.twitter.com/Uugm9L7VnR

The Vikings traded for QB Kirk Cousins on Tuesday, and while I think he'll definitely help by throwing fewer inaccurate passes, I do wonder if he is enough to get this team over the hump. Cousins isn't a spring chicken and has already thrown a lot of passes this season, so his arm might just be shot at this point. If the Vikings can't get a run game going, Cousins might not matter at all.

It's unfortunate that WRs AJ Brown and Romeo Doubs went down with multiple injuries this season, because if any team has needed both of them, it's the New England Patriots. After seemingly finding their groove, the music fell to a screeching halt against Green Bay. Drake Maye had another game of multiple interceptions, and the Patriots lost by 30 points.

Their receiver group has been subpar to this point in the season, leaning on Mack Hollins and Pop Douglas once again. Because there are no easy buttons in this offense, it's all on Maye to keep the offense afloat, and that hasn't gone well this season. They were never going to be in the receiver market this trade deadline, but I wouldn't be surprised if they made a move in free agency, just to give Maye some more help.

I'm sometimes confused by the Steelers' offense. They're at their best when they play through the offensive line, RBs Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle, and the mammoths they have at tight end. But then they try to spread teams out and shred them that way. This doesn't work because the Steelers lack separation on offense, especially at receiver. WR DK Metcalf has been wildly inconsistent this season, mixing in explosive receptions and great blocking with the most baffling drops you've ever seen. WR Michael Pittman Jr. has been on IR since October, and even when he comes back, you don't expect him to be a separator in the offense.

Nobody in the Steelers' receiving room is a big enough threat against man coverage to be a problem, and it shrinks the Rolodex of options the offense can get to in third down or obvious passing situations. Swinging and missing on a receiver at the deadline is brutal, and if they don't win a Super Bowl this year, the skill position group will be why.
