#2627. Re-grading the Jaylen Brown-Paul George trade: Celtics' grade has greatly improved, 76ers' mark stays perfect

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Besides the Luka Dončić stunner, you could argue that this summer's Jaylen Brown blockbuster was the most surprising trade in recent NBA history. A former Finals MVP coming off of his best season traded for ... Paul George? Someone widely treated as one of the NBA's worst contracts and half of the draft capital a superstar typically fetches? The reactions were, obviously, extreme. Celtics fans revolted. Pundits expected a meaningful drop-off for Boston. Trade graders like myself pilloried Brad Stevens and his front office for moving a 29-year-old All-NBA forward for what appeared to be far less than fair value.

And yet, as Brown prepares to face his former employer for the first time, the two teams sit neck-and-neck in the Eastern Conference. The 76ers top the standings at 9-2. The Celtics are right behind them at 8-2, but have the East's best net rating at +11.6. While Philadelphia has thus far gotten exactly what it wanted out of the trade, the Celtics seemingly have as well. So with their first of potentially many high-stakes clashes this season set for Tuesday night (8 p.m. ET, NBC/fubo), let's revisit the trade and hand out revised grades for the offseason's most impactful trade.

The backlash to the George-for-Brown trade was fundamentally centered on two premises:

The first premise was, frankly, outdated in the apron era. Yes, Kevin Durant netted four first-round picks, a first-round swap, and players who would go on to net six additional first-round picks and another swap, but that was all the way back in February 2023, and that trade completely derailed Phoenix's future. The James Harden trade played out similarly for the Nets. Teams are more skittish about all-in moves for older players than they've ever been.

There have been outlier, extremely high-cost trades since then, but all came under somewhat irreplicable circumstances. Mikal Bridges netted five first-round picks and a swap, for instance, but he never misses games, came with two years of cheap cost-control and played collegiately with several other key Knicks. New York viewed him as the finishing piece of a championship team, and the Knicks were ultimately proven correct.

Desmond Bane wasn't as underpaid, but he fit the extremely narrow niche the Magic needed: someone who could enhance their offense without commanding high usage on a team that was already locked into two max-salary shot-creators or compromising their defensive identity. There were maybe a handful of players in the NBA Orlando could have targeted for that role, and Bane, amazingly, was probably the only one available. In an extremely injured Eastern Conference, the Magic tried to be opportunistic. That's where these lopsided trades happen. They're almost always circumstantial.

The more typical star trade scenario is something closer to what the Milwaukee Bucks went through with Giannis Antetokounmpo. The player is older, attempts to fix things internally have failed, and the relationship between star and team is no longer tenable. The acquiring team typically has a leverage advantage, and that's especially true in the apron era, where paying the sort of giant salaries these stars get in their early 30s carries far more risk than reward. Antetokounmpo netted three picks, one swap and a handful of players that won't be foundational for the Bucks. We know Antetokounmpo had more trade value than Brown because the Celtics tried to trade Brown and more for Antetokounmpo, but a deal wasn't struck. So if Antetokounmpo, a two-time MVP, was worth three-and-a-half picks plus some player value, Brown being worth two picks and some player value feels in line with the new, cost-conscious NBA.

And then of course, there's the matter of what the player value actually was. That brings us to George. From November through January of last season, George averaged just 16 points on 42-38-86 shooting. This was in line with his 2024-25 performance, and together, the year-and-a-half sample felt reliable for an aging star. Well, George then got suspended 25 games. When he returned in March, he was a 21-point scorer on better shooting splits who looked rejuvenated defensively. He went on to torch the Celtics in the first round of the playoffs. Most of us expected George to look more like the player he was before that suspension in Boston. The Celtics bet that he would look like who he was after, and thus far, they've looked correct.

The raw numbers are superb: 20.4 points, 47-43-81 shooting and his highest assist and rebounding rates since he left the Clippers. The fit has been even better. Much was made of how low many advanced metrics are on Brown relative to his reputation, but the more significant story here was always his outlier status within Boston's intended team structure. Joe Mazzulla wants to maximize 3-point attempt rate. George's 3-point attempt rate so far this season (51.4%) is nearly twice Brown's (27.8%). Brad Stevens spoke openly about not wanting to concentrate usage in two players, and George's usage rate is nearly eight percentage points lower than Brown's was a year ago. The Celtics wanted this sort of player in their system and next to Jayson Tatum, and it's working.

Yet just as vitally, George is helping the Celtics diversify a bit as a team. The Celtics generated the second-fewest turnovers in the NBA last season. They're averaging the eighth-most in the NBA thus far this season, and George is the single biggest reason why. Only Dyson Daniels and Scottie Barnes are averaging more deflections, and among players who have played at least four games, only Daniels and Kris Dunn are generating more steals.

The Celtics had the lowest free-throw attempt rate in the NBA last season as well. They're right around the middle of the pack this year. Tatum is the one drawing most of those fouls, but George is a critical part of the structure that gets Tatum to the line. Brown can be a bit of a ball-stopper. Among true forwards, only Kawhi Leonard and Zion Williamson averaged more seconds per touch than Brown a year ago. The average George touch this season lasts 3.3 seconds compared to just under five for Brown a year ago. It's simply easier to compromise a defense when the ball is moving and players are making quick decisions. That's how defenses are forced into rotation and wind up fouling out of desperation. As a team, the Celtics have the sixth-lowest average time per touch this season compared to the eighth-highest a year ago.

Even the contract feels a bit more palatable now than it did at the time. Brown would have become eligible for an extension on his supermax contract last offseason, and based on the season he had, he would have been more than justified in asking for one. The Celtics, clearly, had no plans to commit extra years to Brown on top of the three that he was already owed. George isn't quite living up to his supermax price tag thus far this season, but his deal is a year shorter and comes with no such extension pressure.

If anything, his player option for next season opens some interesting doors for the Celtics if they decide they're happy with this partnership. As of right now, the Celtics have around $3 million in first-apron room for the 2027-28 season based on current projections. Say they want to use the full mid-level exception on a free agent or perhaps need a bit more wiggle room to make a trade. They could theoretically go to George and ask him to lower his cap figure in exchange for another year of security. Turning a one-year, $56.6 million deal into, say, a two-year, $90 million deal could make sense for both sides provided George sustains this level of play.

The reasonable fear that he might not is why we stop at a "B-" for Boston. This is still his age-36 season. George has been injury-prone for most of his career. He presumably will not get a 25-game break this season, and even if he's this good all year, all of these benefits he's brought to Boston are somewhat regular-season-centric. The playoffs are a different game, one that leans much more into Brown's strengths as an individual shotmaker and man-to-man defender. The Celtics still never get to the rim. Their best answer for opposing star guards is probably Jordan Walsh, whose offense makes him hard to play for too long. If Boston flames out in the playoffs, we might view Brown's absence as one of the bigger reasons why. The path to actually winning this trade gets paved in April and May.

But for now, at least, it's starting to make sense. The Celtics added two premium draft assets in a way that allowed them to maintain their existing playing style and avoid taking a major step back in the present. They sidestepped what probably would have been an ugly contract negotiation, and the more barbs get traded in the press, the clearer it becomes that this situation simply was not salvageable. The Celtics had to trade Brown. The offers were far lower than we anticipated. Boston still managed to make the best of less-than-ideal circumstances and still factors prominently into the Eastern Conference championship picture.

Funnily enough, you could pretty easily argue that George would actually be a far better fit for this iteration of the 76ers than Brown is. Philadelphia's 20th-ranked offense has a bottom-five 3-point attempt rate and the eighth-highest average seconds per touch in the NBA. The Sixers could stand to trade some of that dribbling for a bit more shooting. Considering how lethal their transition offense can be, George's turnover generation would also fit this defense like a glove. The 76ers will get better offensively. We're still in tiny-sample season, and everyone's still learning how to play together. But George is undeniably the easier player to fit onto a roster like this than Brown.

Of course, the 76ers wouldn't have a roster like this without Brown. Widespread reporting has made it clear that Philadelphia's acquisition of Brown was what first caught the attention of LeBron James in free agency. If Brown was indeed a swing factor in the 76ers getting LeBron, that assuages any short-term salary concerns for Brown. For God's sake, the Philadelphia 76ers have LeBron James on a minimum contract. Even if Brown is overpaid, the surplus value on the James contract more than offsets any negative value there.

The 76ers have far less reason to fear an extension than Boston did as well. By trading Brown, the Celtics subjected him to the NBA's six-month extend-and-trade restrictions. That meant he could only tack one year onto his contract rather than two, and because he has multiple years remaining on his contract, he's not eligible to extend during the season. The 76ers therefore get to table those discussions until the offseason at the earliest, and remember, at that point, Brown will be negotiating off of the more modest statistics that come with sacrificing for the sake of a superteam. It's simply easier to envision Brown extending at less than the max in Philadelphia than it would have been in Boston.

Speaking of sacrificing, remember the whole "Jaylen Brown wants his own team" narrative from last offseason? For all we know, it was true at the time and might have remained true had he stayed with the Celtics. So far, that has been a complete non-issue for the 76ers. Brown is currently sporting his lowest usage rate since 2020 (before he became an All-Star). He's turning the ball over around half as often per 100 possessions as he did a season ago. He's an enormous part of a defense that surprisingly ranks No. 6 in the NBA so far this season. He's even openly called the 76ers Tyrese Maxey's team.

And the 76ers are, obviously, winning. They're mostly winning clutch games, but hey, you expect to win close games with four stars in your starting lineup. They're going to figure out the finer points of maximizing this talent mix over time, but even the "getting to know each other" version of this group poses almost impossible matchup problems for other teams. Take Cleveland, who has already faced Philadelphia twice. Can you guess which two Cavalier defenders have spent the most partial possessions guarding Brown, per NBA.com tracking data? James Harden and Donovan Mitchell, at 60.6 combined. Those are the sort of defenders you try to hide on weak scorers to preserve for offense. Well, where exactly are Harden and Mitchell supposed to hide against this team? There are no weak spots. The advantage of having this many creators is that Philadelphia basically starts every possession with an exploitable mismatch.

On pure talent accumulation alone, this is the sort of roster teams tend to go all-in for. Philadelphia didn't even have to. While the Stepien Rule complicates the tradability of some of their remaining picks, the 76ers are still slated to have four first-round picks in the next seven drafts. There is still ammunition for some sort of pivot here, whether that's a short-term upgrade to maximize this title run or more likely, some sort of long-term change at center as Joel Embiid gets older and potentially less reliable from a health perspective.

There are going to be depth questions down the line. Even if Brown gets less than a 35% max on his eventual extension, he's going to be pricey. Maxey feels like a near-lock for a supermax extension in the years to come, and while VJ Edgecombe will almost certainly be limited to 25% of the cap on his rookie extension, he'll still account for quite a bit of money. The 76ers are a top-heavy roster today, and that's after hitting a few home runs on the margins and getting arguably the greatest player of all time to take the minimum. Sustaining contention beyond the "Embiid is still a matchup nightmare and LeBron is on the team" era is going to require near-perfect management on the margins.

But this isn't rocket science. How many teams have a trio they can feel better about for, say, the next three-to-five years than Maxey, Brown and Edgecombe? The Brown trade opened an immediate championship window and likely ensured a relatively high baseline for the rest of the decade, assuming acceptable health and wise decisions elsewhere on the roster. It was a great trade in July and it remains a great trade today.

#2626. Bob Boone, All-Star catcher, 1980 World Series champion and father of Yankees manager, dies at 78

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Bob Boone, a four-time All-Star catcher and the middle member of a three-generation baseball family, has died. He was 78. His son, Bret Boone, made the announcement on Tuesday. No cause of death was given.

My dad- He was my mentor, my coach, my rock. He taught me how to be a pro and more importantly, how to be a man. He was one of the highest integrity people I’ve ever known and I’m going to miss him dearly. Baseball lost a great one yesterday. R.I.P dad, I love you❤️ pic.twitter.com/4NtYAwXIv3

"Bob Boone had an enduring impact on the field as a 19-year MLB veteran, a seven-time Gold Glove Award-winning catcher, a four-time All-Star and 1980 World Champion with the Philadelphia Phillies," the MLB Players Association said in a statement. "He embraced a leadership role in the Players Association early in his career, and earned a reputation as a strong and principled voice in the advancement of player rights in the 1970s and '80s ... As we honor Bob's legacy and mourn his passing, we extend our heartfelt condolences to his wife, Sue, sons Aaron, Bret and Matt, his extended family, and his many fans and admirers throughout the game."

The Boones were baseball's first three-generation family. Bob's father, Ray Boone, played for six teams from 1948-60, and his sons Aaron and Bret both had long careers spanning the 1990s and 2000s. Bob's other son, Matt, played in the minor leagues.

"I'm just so grateful that I had a dad that took us to work with him all the time," Aaron, now manager of the New York Yankees, said in 2023 (via MLB.com). "He came up at the end of '72, and I was born in the spring of '73. He played until my senior year in high school and literally I was at the ballpark -- my brothers and I, in unis, shagging (fly balls) and doing everything you could possibly imagine. It was a great way to grow up."

Born in San Diego, Bob Boone made his MLB debut with the Phillies in 1972 and took over as the club's starting catcher in 1973. He hit 10 home runs and finished third in the National League Rookie of the Year voting. That started a 17-year run as one of the game's best and most durable catchers. Boone started at least 130 games behind the plate eight times in his career and 110 games 14 times.

With the Phillies in 1980, Boone went 7 for 17 (.412) with four walks and zero strikeouts in Philadelphia's six-game World Series win over the Kansas City Royals.

A seven-time Gold Glove winner, including four straight during his age-38 to -41 seasons, Boone had his most productive years with the Phillies from 1976-79. He hit .282/.351/.414 those four seasons and averaged nine home runs, which was excellent output given the offensive standard at the catcher position during that era. Boone went to four All-Star Games and received MVP votes twice.

"Bob was an incredible player, teammate and family man," the Phillies said in a statement. "He embodied everything we believe exemplary athletes should represent, both on and off the field. We were proud to have him as part of the Phillies family during one of the most historic runs in team history. His impact on our organization, his teammates, and everyone who had the privilege of knowing him will never be forgotten."

Boone ranks second with 2,161 games at catcher during the Modern Era (since 1900), behind only Hall of Famer Ivan Rodriguez (2,377). He is 15th among primary catchers with 1,838 hits and 21st with 2,508 total bases. Boone played parts of 19 big league seasons with the Phillies (1972-81), California Angels (1982-88), and Royals (1989-90).

The Orlando SunRays, a potential expansion franchise, hired Boone to be their manager soon after he retired as a player, though the expansion franchises were instead awarded to Denver and Miami in 1991. Boone later managed the Royals from 1995-97 and the Cincinnati Reds (2001-03). He managed his son, Aaron, those years with the Reds.

In 2005, Boone joined the Washington Nationals as their director of player development and had a hand in building the core that won the franchise's first World Series title in 2019. He remained with the Nationals until 2021. Boone spent five years on the Hall of Fame ballot from 1996 to 2000 but was not voted into Cooperstown.

#2625. NFL midseason grades, awards, 2nd-half predictions; Commanders open up NFC East race

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

Nine of the NFL's 18 weeks are in the books. The halfway point is still far too soon to tell the whole story of the season, but we do have a good idea as to which teams will make the strongest Super Bowl pushes and which players will define the campaign. Our NFL staff took everything that unfolded in the first half of the season to issue team report cards and also to look forward to the award races and championship picture. Picks are in for MVP, Coach of the Year, the Super Bowl and more.

The biggest landslide among our panel of voters came in the Protector of the Year deliberations. Of the 15 voters, 12 selected Lions tackle Penei Sewell as the top offensive lineman. Our Zach Pereles explained why he is the runaway favorite.

Rookie of the Year is a dead heat on both sides of the ball. Defensively, there are only two real candidates: Arvell Reese and David Bailey. But on offense, it's still a much more open race. Each of these players received votes:

1. Browns WR Denzel Boston (7 votes) 2. Broncos RB Jonah Coleman (3) T3. Titans WR Carnell Tate, Raiders QB Fernando Mendoza (2) 5. Browns WR KC Concepcion (1)

As for the Super Bowl picture, the Jaguars are the staff's favorites while the Bears and 49ers are the strongest contenders. Our John Breech has his eyes on someone else, though. Take a look at his full playoff projections and his championship pick. And beyond these, Beech makes some bold predictions for the second half that will bring the NFC West down a peg or two.

One of two Big Ten teams will effectively be eliminated from College Football Playoff contention in a massive Week 11 game at 3:30 p.m. ET on CBS. The clash between No. 9 Indiana and No. 18 USC is easily one of the biggest games in the conference thus far and headlines college football's Saturday slate.

Both sides are still alive in the Big Ten title race. Indiana maintains control of its own destiny, but this is a must-win for USC, which has just a 9% chance of reaching the final conference championship game. Our David Cobb picked the Trojans to cover the 7.5-point spread, but can they win outright? It would be a potentially pivotal victory for Lincoln Riley in his underwhelming tenure if so.

Another Big Ten matchup is the source of Tom Fornelli's Lock of the Week.

Meanwhile, in the SEC, No. 6 Texas heads to Death Valley, where it is always difficult to win at night. No. 21 LSU is a four-point favorite at home. A road favorite elsewhere in the conference is on upset alert. No. 8 Tennessee (-2.5 at Texas A&M) is one team we're keeping an eye on in a possible letdown spot.

We're in the throes of spooky season, and fittingly, the New Jersey Devils just got a lot scarier with the acquisition of superstar goaltender Connor Hellebuyck.

Moving forward, the Devils will be burdened with the pressure that comes along with being a bona fide Cup contender. For a franchise that's fallen short of expectations a few times lately, that can be a scary prospect, and it inspired a special Halloween edition of the NHL Power Rankings in which I highlight the scariest thing about each team.

#2623. Cooper Flagg beats LeBron James, Anthony Edwards to NBA history: How the Mavericks star leveled up

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

With just over 30 seconds to play on Monday, Naji Marshall missed a free throw that would have put the Dallas Mavericks up by three, but secured the offensive rebound and kicked the ball out to Cooper Flagg. The 2026 Rookie of the Year took some time to assess the situation, then jab-stepped to his right and drove left. He took two dribbles and rose up over Andrew Nembhard, who could do little but hope he missed.

Flagg did not miss. His mid-range jumper was pure and put the Mavericks up by four with 26 seconds left in an eventual 125-122 win over the Indiana Pacers. Flagg, who had been knocked out of the Mavericks' previous matchup with the Pacers this season by a flagrant foul from Aaron Nesmith, finished with a season-high 43 points, 10 rebounds, six assists and three steals on 16 of 25 from the field as the Mavericks won their third game in a row to improve to 7-4.

In the process, Flagg became the first teenager in NBA history to record five 40-point games -- as many as LeBron James and Anthony Edwards combined. No one else besides those three has more than one 40-point game as a teenager. In addition, Flagg is now third all-time in total points scored before turning 20, behind only Kobe Bryant and James. Furthermore, Flagg joined Kevin Durant as the only teenagers to have a 40-point, 10-rebound, five-assist game.

For the season, Flagg is now averaging 25.9 points, 6.9 rebounds, 6.9 assists and 2.2 steals, and that's despite leaving the first game against the Pacers early and an ice-cold 3 of 19 performance against the Sacramento Kings. He's 11th in the league in scoring, 16th in assists and fifth in steals.

"He affects the game in so many ways, and he makes the right plays as far as passing. Thank goodness he's on our team," Mavericks coach Dusty May said after Monday's win. "It's unbelievable he's a 19-year-old doing this."

As May noted, Flagg is far more than just a scorer. But as he continues to establish himself as one of the best young scorers in NBA history, let's take a closer look at how he gets it done in that department.

Flagg is 6-foot-9 and uses his size to get to the basket on a regular basis. He doesn't just bully opponents, though; he plays with a pace that's rare for his age, has great craft around the rim, and is more than willing to move off the ball. You need to look no further than Monday's outing against the Pacers to see how many different ways Flagg can score around the rim.

He forced his way to the rim out of isolation, threw down a dunk in transition, attacked a closeout for another slam, cut back door and spun into another layup, drove to the basket out of the pick-and-roll, cut back door again for an easy finish and ran in transition for a double-clutch lefty finger roll.

Flagg is taking six shots at the rim per game, per Synergy Sports, and shooting 61.7% on them. Among players that have taken at least 50 attempts at the rim this season, Flagg ranks 20th in efficiency.

His ability to get into the paint also helps him earn trips to the free-throw line, where he's shooting 90.3%. Flagg's 7.2 free throw attempts per game rank 12th in the league, and are up from 4.9 per game as a rookie. In his rookie season, Flagg only had eight games with double-digit free throw attempts; he has three already this season.

Flagg put in extensive work on his mid-range game during the offseason, and it's paying major dividends to start the season. Not only has he increased his scoring output, but he's done so while taking less punishment.

"I think just being able to get to my spots at a higher level, and being more comfortable with that, has allowed me to take a little bit of load off my body. Just kind of stopping short, raising up over people," Flagg said on Monday. "It's taxing to get downhill all the way to the rim and try and finish over seven-footers all night, every night. Just adding that in there definitely allows me to pace myself a little bit, steal some easy ones."

Flagg's two clutch buckets late in the win over the Pacers were a perfect example of his improvement.

Flagg is 25 of 42 on off-the-dribble 2-point attempts this season. Among the seven players who have taken at least 40 such attempts, no one has been more efficient. While Flagg isn't going to shoot nearly 60% on pull-up 2s all season, it's clear that he's far more comfortable with his in-between game, which is a great sign for his development.

"He's able to square in the air from 15, 17 feet. He can get to his spots, and if there's a smaller guy he can just jump and square in the air over them," May said.

Flagg's growth inside the arc has allowed him to increase his scoring average by nearly five points per game despite the fact that his 3-point shot remains a work in progress. After shooting 29.5% as a rookie, he's shooting 29.2% this season on slightly more attempts.

Flagg is shooting 30.8% on catch-and-shoot attempts and 31.6% on off-the-dribble attempts. Notably, he's also at just 31.6% on wide-open attempts.

"Like the 3-point percentage obviously hasn't been great, but I still trust myself," Flagg said on Sunday. "I think my teammates trust me, my coaches. So I'm gonna keep shooting it, and I worked on it all summer. I worked on it all last year, so I'm not worried about anything."

Flagg did shoot 38.5% from behind the arc in his lone collegiate season at Duke. That, combined with his elite free throw shooting, suggests that he won't be a sub-30% 3-point shooter forever. If Flagg does eventually become a more reliable shooter, that would be bad news for the rest of the league.

In the last couple of games, he's made some 3s, and he's making all his free throws.

"That's how you put up the 43 points, where you do a little bit of everything," May said after Monday's game. "He finished at the mid-range, he finished at the rim, he got to the line. He's getting to the line more than he has. He affects the game in so many ways, and he makes the right plays as far as passing. Thank goodness he's on our team. It's unbelievable he's a 19-year-old doing this."

#2622. MLB rumors: Mets to meet with Tarik Skubal, Rangers' Corey Seager plan, plus Blue Jays, Cubs, Red Sox, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is an important week on the baseball calendar. First and foremost, it is awards week. Kevin McGonigle and Sal Stewart were named the Rookies of the Year on Monday. The Managers of the Year will be announced Tuesday, Cy Youngs and Relievers of the Year will be announced Wednesday, and finally the MVPs will be announced Thursday.

Also, the GM Meetings are this week in Las Vegas. The GM Meetings are not the Winter Meetings in terms of the sheer volume of rumors and transactions, but they do usually provide some news. There could be more than usual this year given the near certainty of a lockout on Dec. 1, which would also mean there are no Winter Meetings. This may be the only time everyone is in the same room this winter. The three weeks between now and Dec. 1 could be quite active.

We've already ranked the top 50 free agents and the top 25 trade candidates.

With that in mind, here are Tuesday's hot stove rumors.

The Mets have a meeting scheduled with two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, the clear top free agent avaiable this offseason, later this week, reports the New York Post. Skubal will meet with teams in California, presumably at the offices of agent Scott Boras. Owner Steve Cohen is expected to push for Skubal, according to SNY; president of baseball operations David Stearns has long been reluctant to sign big-money, long-term deals for pitchers, though pitchers of Skubal's caliber are rarely available. The Mets are also seeking first base help and bullpen reinforcements.

Nolan McLean and Christian Scott are the only locks for New York's 2027 rotation at the moment. Justin Hagenman, Sean Manaea, Kodai Senga, Zac Thornton, and Jonah Tong are next in line to make starts. Tylor Megill is expected back from Tommy John surgery early next year as well. The Mets have some depth but clearly need more impact.

The Rangers signed Corey Seager to a 10-year, $325 million deal prior to the 2022 season and it paid off quite handsomely with a World Series title in 2023 (Seager was the World Series MVP). With five years and roughly $155 million left on the deal, however, the Rangers appear ready to trade him.

The Rangers "intend to explore moving Seager at the general managers' meetings," reports The Athletic.

Seager, 32, was stellar from 2023 to 2025 in spite of a litany of injuries, averaging 6.2 WAR per season with a .294 average and 158 OPS+. He actually averaged 8.7 WAR per 162 games. Only the injuries kept him from making multiple serious MVP runs. Last season, though, was a step back. In 102 games, he hit .227/.312/.424 with 20 home runs, 51 RBI and 3.1 WAR.

The injury history keeps getting more extensive, too, as he's dealt with injuries to his thumb, hamstring, hip, other hamstring and back in the last four years.

With a lackluster, at best, shortstop class in free agency, now might be the perfect time for the Rangers to move on from Seager, assuming a deal can be worked out with the years and dollars left on his contract. Texas also has Sebastian Walcott, one of the top prospects in baseball, ready in the wings.

The Blue Jays are among the teams with interest in free agent second baseman Brandon Lowe, according to Sportsnet. Ernie Clement, Toronto's primary second baseman in 2026, crashed hard in the second half and has always fit better as a super utility man who plays regularly at different positions. Josh Smith is the team's other second base option.

Lowe would bring needed power to a team that finished dead last in home runs this past season and had just one player, Kazuma Okamoto (33), clear 15 home runs. Only four Blue Jays hit even 10 homers. Also, Toronto's lineup is mostly right-handed. Lowe would add power and also a lefty bat to provide balance. We ranked him as the 13th-best free agent available.

Adding rotation help is a "top priority," White Sox GM Chris Getz said during an MLB Network Radio interview on Tuesday. "We're going to exhaust the starter market, both free agency -- we'll take a look -- along with trades. That is our top priority," Getz said. He also confirmed that Grant Taylor, the team's postseason closer, will move into the rotation. Hagen Smith will remain in the bullpen.

The White Sox have solid enough rotation depth with Taylor joining Sean Burke, Luis Castillo, Anthony Kay, Davis Martin, David Sandlin, Noah Schultz, and perhaps Shane Smith and Drew Thorpe. There is room for improvement, though, particularly at the top. Chicago could use a bona fide ace, not that one is easy to acquire or abundantly available.

Add the Padres to the list of teams that have shown interest in Skubal, reports MLB Network. San Diego has a major need in the rotation -- Joe Musgrove, who hasn't made a start since the 2024 postseason, and Randy Vásquez are their only rotation locks -- and a new ownership group that seems willing to spend in its first offseason.

Skubal is far and away the offseason's best free agent. He is also a Scott Boras client, and, historically, top Boras clients take the largest contract offer regardless of team situation. That isn't to say the Padres are a bad situation. Not at all. They're a very good team that is in the postseason most years, plus they play in San Diego. Who doesn't love San Diego?

The Padres are also connected to several Japanese players, according to The Athletic. That includes MLB free agents Seiya Suzuki and Shota Imanaga, as well as players coming over from Nippon Professional Baseball, like third baseman Teruaki Sato.

Free agent lefty Adrian Morejon is drawing interest as a starting pitcher, but he prefers to remain in the bullpen, according to The Athletic. Even during the season, there were rumblings that Morejon would like to be given a chance to start in 2027. He came up through the minors as a starter and only remained in the bullpen because he was so dominant in a late-inning role.

We ranked Morejon as the offseason's second-best free agent on the idea that he would move into the rotation. The belief within the game is that he has a chance to be an excellent starter, not just a back-end piece. Either way, Morejon is a very good pitcher, and at 28, he's also one of the youngest free agents available. He should have several peak years remaining.

Although they are disinclined to pursue Tarik Skubal, the Cubs hope to add three established starting pitchers this offseason, reports The Athletic. Of the nine pitchers to make at least nine starts for Chicago in 2027, seven are free agents. Only Ben Brown, who recently had neck surgery (per ESPN), and Edward Cabrera, who had a 5.96 ERA and was demoted to the bullpen, remain.

Left-hander Justin Steele is expected back from UCL surgery next year, though he suffered a setback this summer and wasn't able to return as hoped in September. Others like Javier Assad and Jordan Wicks are depth options more than full-time rotation pieces. This free agent class offers plenty of second- and third-tier starters. That's where the Cubs are expected to shop.

Unlike last offseason, the Mets are not interested in a major overhaul despite their disappointing year, reports MLB.com. The Mets went 74-88 and finished in last place in 2026. The only silver lining to the disappointing season was the ability to give a long runway to rookies like Carson Benge and Nolan McLean, both of whom finished in the top four of the Rookie of the Year voting.

The Mets went 83-79 in 2025 and missed the postseason on the final day of the season. They made significant changes last winter, most notably jettisoning stalwarts Pete Alonso and Brandon Nimmo, then had a worse season in 2026. In September, president of baseball operations David Stearns admitted that much turnover created an "uncapped downside scenario," which is executive-speak for "there was too much risk."

Not surprisingly, the Braves are uninterested in moving former National League MVP Ronald Acuña Jr., according to MLB Network. It does feel like Atlanta's offense has gone stale and that they could move a core piece, but it won't be Acuña, nor is it likely to be Drake Baldwin, Michael Harris II, or Matt Olson. Ozzie Albies and Austin Riley are the more obvious players to move. Albies is entering the final season of his wildly team-friendly contract. Riley has six years remaining on his deal, which figures to make a move difficult.

On Monday, Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow declined to commit to Trevor Story as his starting shortstop next season. "We still have a ton of confidence in Trevor, but any decisions like that are going to take place between Trevor and me far before I speak to anything publicly," Breslow told reporters, including the Boston Globe. Boston has one of the top prospects in the minors in shortstop Franklin Arias, who is very likely to make his debut early next year. Arias could push Story into a utility role or off the team entirely.

#2620. "It's a huge honour" – Uli Hoeneß added into German football's Hall of Fame

Former FC Bayern Munich and Germany icon Uli Hoeneß has expressed his gratitude at being added to the Hall of Fame of German football.

“It's a huge honour to be inducted into the German Football Hall of Fame," Hoeneß said in an in-house interview at Bayern.

"I'll never forget my time as a player – it was the best time of my life: the moment we won the European Cup for the first time with FC Bayern in 1974 – the world could have stopped for me!

"I'm incredibly grateful to football for everything it has given me, and it's always been important to me to give something back.

"When I look at FC Bayern today, I think our fans can be proud: successful on the pitch, financially stable, and extremely socially committed.

#2618. Blue Jays executive responds to Anthony Santander's 'extremely disappointing' anti-Muslim social media posts

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Blue Jays general manager Ross Atkins had strong words Tuesday in reaction to Anthony Santander's anti-Muslim social media posts that he has since deleted.

"There really aren't words to express my level of disappointment," Atkins said from the GM meetings on Tuesday, via Sportsnet. "Anything exacerbating some level of hate, anti-Islamic, is just extremely concerning and extremely disappointing.

"I also talked to Anthony about his lack of awareness, realizing that he has a very large microphone, what that meant. We're working exceptionally hard internally to ensure, and we have been, that it's a safe environment, that baseball is for everyone. It's very important to us. It's a part of our organizational values and his behavior did not align with that."

Santander, a native Venezuelan, shared social media videos in the wake of the U.S. midterm elections last week, including one where a Christian pastor said, "there is no such thing as kind Muslims." Another implied that Sharia law would be imposed in the U.S. following the election of Abdul El-Sayed to the Senate. Santander has since taken down the videos from his social media pages.

In the aftermath, the team released the following statement:

"Baseball is for everyone, and the Blue Jays have created an inclusive experience where all fans feel welcome at our ballpark. Individual comments do not represent our organization's values and beliefs."

It's unclear whether Santander plans to address the matter publicly, but Atkins said he "told him that I thought he needed to and that he should."

As far as personal conversations with Santander, Atkins said, "I expressed my level of concern. I believe he felt it. I know he feels badly. But I don't want to speak for him."

Santander was signed as an amateur free agent out of Venezuela in 2011 when he was 16. He signed a free agent deal with the Blue Jays prior to the 2025 season; injuries have held him to just 54 games in the past two seasons.

#2615. 2026 MLB Manager of the Year: White Sox's Will Venable, Brewers' Pat Murphy win BBWAA awards

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Chicago White Sox manager Will Venable and Brewers manager Pat Murphy were named the Managers of the Year in their respective leagues on Tuesday night as part of the BBWAA's awards week. Murphy is the first manager to ever win the award in three consecutive seasons.

The annual awards, which also include Manager of the Year, Reliever of the Year, Cy Young and MVP, are voted on by 30 members of the Baseball Writers Association of America (that's two per MLB city in each league). Votes were submitted before the beginning of the playoffs, meaning that only regular-season contributions are taken into account.

Murphy, manager of the World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers, has been voted the National League Manager of the Year, the Baseball Writers Association of America announced on Tuesday. He is the first person to win three consecutive Manager of the Year awards and the tenth person with three Manager of the Year wins in total.

Ballots for the BBWAA's awards are submitted between the end of the regular season and the beginning of the postseason. They are regular-season awards and Milwaukee's World Series win did not factor into the voting.

Of course, Murphy did not need the World Series win to boost his Manager of the Year case. He guided the small-market Brewers to baseball's best record (103-59) and run differential (+214) during the regular season, and their fourth consecutive NL Central title. Their 103 wins are a franchise record and baseball's most since 2023.

Murphy just completed his third season as Brewers manager and has three Manager of the Year wins to show for it. Bobby Cox (2004-05), Kevin Cash (2020-21), and Stephen Vogt (2024-25) are the only others with two consecutive Manager of the Year awards. Vogt was not an American League Manager of the Year finalist this season.

Prior to Murphy's threepeat here, the Brewers had never had a Manager of the Year winner. He's won the award now three times in three years at the helm.

Atlanta Braves manager Walt Weiss and Philadelphia Phillies manager Don Mattingly finished behind Murphy in the voting. Mattingly took over as an interim after the Phillies fired Rob Thomson on April 28. Philadelphia had baseball's fourth-best record after the managerial change. Weiss guided the Braves to the NL East title.

Venable, who helped orchestrate a 24-win year-to-year improvement and guided the team to its first postseason berth since 2021, has been named the American League Manager of the Year, the Baseball Writers Association of America announced on Tuesday. He beat out Tampa Bay Rays manager Kevin Cash and Boston Red Sox manager Chad Tracy.

The White Sox went 84-78 in 2026 after going 60-102 in 2025 and a hideous 41-121 in 2024. Those 121 losses are the record in baseball's Modern Era (since 1900). Venable's White Sox are the first team in history to reach the postseason after losing at least 100 games in the previous two seasons (they also lost 101 games in 2023).

The huge steps forward seem to be what secured the award for Venable. He took over in 2025 and the White Sox improved by 19 wins that season, only to turn around and improve by 24 more wins this past season. They were arguably the most surprising playoff team in 2026 and Venable gets his due here.

Venable joins the following White Sox manager of the year winners:

Cash finishes as the runner-up in a very close vote. Venable got 15 of the 30 first-place votes while Cash got 12. Tracy finishes in third place, with Guardians manager Stephen Vogt fourth and Yankees' skipper Aaron Boone sitting fifth.

Cash's Rays improved by 21 games to win an AL-best 98 and win the AL East after finishing in fourth place in 2025. Tracy took over the Red Sox after Alex Cora started 10-17 and was fired. Tracy went 77-58 and earned the second AL wild card.

#2614. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2612. Celtics vs. 76ers winners and losers: Jayson Tatum outduels Jaylen Brown, but Paul George steals the show

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Nick Nurse nailed it. A lot of people had a lot to say in advance of the Celtics and 76ers facing each other for the first time this season, but Philadelphia's coach summed it up pretty well before the two teams tipped off on Tuesday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

"This is probably one -- maybe the one -- that people were circling in the summertime when the schedule came out," Nurse said.

Nick Nurse on his morning conversation with Jaylen Brown and hype surrounding the grudge match with the Celtics.“This is probably one — maybe the one — that people were circling in the summer time when the schedule came out. It’s finally here.” pic.twitter.com/CdBoE576iI

He wasn't kidding. From the moment Jaylen Brown was traded to the Sixers, the hype and drama surrounding the first meeting between him and his old team -- and his longtime running mate-turned-rival, Jayson Tatum -- have been seemingly endless. While Tatum tried to lower the heat on the simmering feud, claiming that he was "caught off guard as much as the rest of the world" when Brown was shipped to Philly, Brown was all too happy to add rhetorical fuel to the fire, saying there might not be beef between the two players, but there was some "lamb chops and gravy" and warning his former teammate to "stay ready at all times."

By Tuesday, there wasn't much left unsaid. When Brown was asked whether he would talk to Tatum prior to the game, he dismissed the idea: "There's nothing to talk about. He's on his side, I'm on my side. We're playing basketball. Both of us are trying to win. So there's nothing to talk about. Check the ball up."

The old saying about being careful what you wish for comes to mind. They checked the ball up and the Celtics ran the Sixers off their floor in what ended up as a blowout 123-101 win for Boston. Aside from the actual victory for the Celtics that moved them ahead of the Sixers in the standings and into first place in the Eastern Conference, here are the winners and losers from the most anticipated game of the season to date, including the under-discussed player in the Brown-to-Philly deal having the performance of the night.

The Sixers beating the Celtics in the first round of the playoffs last year was the outlier, not the rule. Boston tends to get the better of Philly in big games. Tatum and the Celtics reminded everyone about that on Tuesday. He finished with 21 points, six rebounds, four assists and two blocks. And a whole lot of bragging rights.

We got some Tatum vs. Brown one-on-one matchups early, with Tatum getting the better of the duel at the defensive end.

Jayson Tatum forces the turnover on Jaylen Brown in their first iso of the game.📺 NBA on NBC and Peacock pic.twitter.com/IOStW8Kk93

And while his most memorable play didn't come against Brown, Tatum still had the highlight of the evening when he threw down a monster dunk on LeBron James.

JAYSON TATUM WITH THE POSTER ON LEBRON JAMES!📺 NBA on NBC and Peacock pic.twitter.com/LOXzzT0FjJ

Brown was right. There wasn't anything left to talk about. Tatum did his talking on the court.

This was always going to be a zero-sum game. Tatum won, Brown lost. But the way Brown went down wasn't great as far as optics and narratives go. He was held to a season-low 13 points, got in foul trouble, had four turnovers and was a game-worst minus-27. Oof.

Apart from a nice dunk in the first half, it was a game for Brown to forget. Making matters worse, the guy he got traded for had a night to remember.

"I'm a bit frustrated, honestly," Brown said after the game. "I wanted to perform better for my team. Foul trouble kind of derailed me a little bit, but it happens. It's unfortunate, but now we got to just move on to the next."

When the Sixers traded George, it seemed like a magic trick by new president of basketball operations Mike Gansey. George played just 78 largely unspectacular games over two seasons in Philly. Beyond that, he's six years older than Brown and still had two years and more than $110 million left on his deal.

So naturally, George has looked like the best version of himself since leaving Philly and going to Boston. His hot start to the season continued on Tuesday with him dropping 36 points on 14 for 22 shooting from the field, including making six of his 11 3-point attempts. He was so good against his former team that at one point he inspired NBC's Noah Eagle on the play-by-play call to exclaim, "PG-13 has turned Rated R." (Prepackaged, but still a great line.)

PAUL GEORGE HAS 30 POINTSVINTAGE PG. 🔥🔥🔥 pic.twitter.com/AH8RI4yVnp

It was supposed to be either Tatum or Brown's night, but George ended up commanding the biggest spotlight with how well he played. He also got the last laugh after an interaction with a Philly fan who, according to George, "dropped the ball on the ground like I'm a dog to go fetch or go get it instead of passing the ball to me like a normal fan." In response, George said he "rolled him a middle finger."

Looks like Paul George may have also flipped out a fan (or someone) after that three pic.twitter.com/LecXldKldE

With Brad Stevens in the front office and Joe Mazzulla on the sideline, the Celtics have long had a theory of the case: Take more 3s than their opponents and bet that they'll make more. That gamble has served them well more often than not. They won a championship that way while leading the league in 3-point attempts and makes per game during the 2023-24 season. The strategy did not work as well against the Sixers in the last postseason, but the Celtics have made peace with the approach, win or lose.

Nothing has changed. Boston still loves to fire away from deep, and that's exactly what the Celtics did against the Sixers on Tuesday. Boston shot 45% from beyond the arc (22 for 49), compared to just 30% for Philadelphia (11 for 37).

When the outside shots are falling for the Celtics, they're tough to beat. No one knows that better than Jaylen Brown.

Why shake hands or hug when you can just turn your back and offer a cold shoulder instead?

The pregame moment between Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown.📺 NBA on NBC and Peacock pic.twitter.com/P4iclUnqZ5

When asked about this moment, Brown told reporters he "wasn't paying attention" when Tatum attempted to greet him.

"I'm just focused on coming out and doing what's best for my team. Everything else was just, to be honest, I wasn't paying attention," Brown said. "Credit to Jayson, he played well tonight. Credit to the Celtics, they executed, they shot the hell out of the ball and were the better team tonight."

Arguably the best part of Brown ignoring Tatum was Tatum then immediately going to LeBron James for an intricate handshake and embrace right afterward.

Looks like Jayson Tatum tried to dap up/hug Jaylen Brown but it wasn’t reciprocated pic.twitter.com/6iMOrpvmmD

Pretty much everyone was asked about Tatum and Brown, from Joe Mazzulla talking about how the trade could have been handled differently, to Payton Pritchard weighing in on whether there was beef between them, to Paul George taking credit for helping the Sixers "land a future piece" in Brown by getting traded (all the lols there).

The winner, though, was 76ers guard Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, who, unlike Pritchard, didn't try to minimize the suspected animosity between Tatum and Brown -- or at least what appears to be some obvious hurt feelings from Brown's side. When Caldwell-Pope was asked about the situation, he pointed to a social media interaction as proof of what we all suspected anyway.

"I don't know what the tension was before JB left," Caldwell-Pope said. "All I know is when he wrote on the comments when JT did that little interview, that's all I know. That's all I need to know."

Kentavious Caldwell-Pope says Jaylen Brown mindset going into the matchup with the Celtics is he’s trying to BTA:“I don’t know what the tension was before but before JB left all I know is when he wrote on the comments when JT did that little interview, that’s all I know, that’s… pic.twitter.com/Co8Wkh0APS

If you somehow missed it, "that little interview" was Tatum claiming that he found out about the trade when everyone else did -- which prompted Brown to pop up in the comments with a cap emoji, essentially calling Tatum a liar. Credit to Caldwell-Pope for calling it like it is rather than pretending.

Speaking of pretending, Nurse was asked about how Brown was approaching the game and reached into his bag of coach clichés for a classic favored by so many in his profession during times like these.

"He's approaching it as another game," Nurse said. "Big game. He's excited for the opportunity, but he wasn't expressing it in a personal way. He said this is a really good test for our team, and I agree with him."

Nick Nurse on how Jaylen Brown is approaching tonight’s game:“He's approaching it as another game. Big game. He's excited for the opportunity, but he wasn't expressing it in a personal way. He said this is a really good test for our team, and I agree with him.” pic.twitter.com/6MiBQXBVCx

Brown advised Tatum to stay ready at all times and everyone from the fans to the media dined out on the pork chops and gravy remarks for weeks in advance. It's hard to sell that as just another game.

Full marks to whoever came up with the song selection for Celtics shootaround on Tuesday.

Celtics shootaround underway with “why can’t we be friends” playing. pic.twitter.com/EJV3A8pQKL

Not long before tip-off, ESPN's Shams Charania reported that Tatum and Brown had a "heart-to-heart" in France prior to the trade. According to the report, the meeting occurred shortly after Brown was dangled in a failed trade attempt for Giannis Antetokounmpo, but before he was sent to Philadelphia.

That sounded pretty juicy, except to hear longtime NBA guard Evan Turner tell it on social media, "this didn't happen." Not to be outdone, Carmelo Anthony also weighed in on the topic, saying that being around the two in France was "weird."

Carmelo Anthony says the energy was weird with Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown in France when they we're all together just days before the trade happened pic.twitter.com/NQ0rGnt5Vh

Turner's source on the subject was unclear, but he was pretty emphatic about the denial, insisting in the comments to the story that the pair never spoke. Not sure that anyone predicted Turner coming off the top rope to smack down an NBA report, but if this ends with him or Carmelo becoming the new Woj, we're all in for a treat.

#2611. Astros name franchise icon Brad Ausmus as new manager as Houston tries to turn back the clock

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Houston Astros have chosen Brad Ausmus as their next manager, the team announced on Wednesday

Ausmus replaces Joe Espada, whose contract as Houston manager was not renewed after three seasons. Espada led the Astros to the playoffs in two of those seasons.

"I am very excited to be back in Houston," Ausmus said in a statement. "The Astros and the city of Houston have been a huge part of my life, and I'm thrilled to create a new chapter as the team's manager. I'd like to thank [general manager Randy Flores] and the entire Astros organization for this opportunity, and I can't wait to get to work."

Ausmus, 57, had served as bench coach for the New York Yankees since late 2023. Prior to that, he had two stints as a big-league manager. He first managed the Detroit Tigers from 2014-17, and over that span he guided the team to a 314-332 record and a division title in his first season. Ausmus also managed the Angels to a 72-90 record in 2019. Overall, Ausmus as a manager has a winning percentage of .478 in five seasons.

Before his dugout career, Ausmus was a top defensive catcher for years. Ausmus's playing career spanned parts of 18 seasons in Major League Baseball, 10 of which came with the Astros. Along the way, Ausmus won three Gold Gloves behind the mask and earned an All-Star selection as a member of the Tigers in 1999.

"We are thrilled to welcome Brad back to the Astros organization," Flores said in a statement. "Brad impressed us throughout the interview process, demonstrating the leadership, energy, and expertise critical to driving a winning culture both on and off the field. I am excited to work alongside Brad and happy to have him back in an Astros uniform."

With Houston, Ausmus is the first major hire undertaken by Flores, who himself was named to his post earlier in the offseason. The Astros are coming off a division title and a postseason berth in 2026. However, they also finished 81-81 and had a negative run differential. It's an uncertain future, as the Astros have an aging roster in spots, a weak farm system, and multiple core contributors entering their walk years in 2027.

It remains to be seen whether owner Jim Crane will try to wring out another season of contention from the roster or lean into a rebuild. Whatever the course, Ausmus will help guide it in a city where he remains a highly popular figure.

As of Houston's decision to hire Ausmus, the Los Angeles Angels are the only team with a current managerial vacancy. Earlier in the offseason, the Philadelphia Phillies retained interim manager Don Mattingly on a permanent basis, as did the New York Mets with Andy Green, and the Seattle Mariners replaced Dan Wilson with Jason Kanzler.

#2607. At MLB GM Meetings, the Phillies are at a crossroads while the Mets have a clear priority

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

LAS VEGAS — The Phillies are at a crossroads. A team that is still full of promise. A team that can compete with some of the best clubs in the league. A team that has World Series hopes. But also a team whose core consists of aging superstars.

"We have a lot of high-end salary players, and they're not young, they're not old, but they're in that age bracket that you have to make a decision," Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowksi said Tuesday during GM Meetings. "Maybe we have enough high-end players, and we need to complement them with other players overall. That's a decision we have to make."

With a likely lockout looming and the financial structure of baseball's future unclear, the Phillies have a projected payroll of $247 million for 2027. Roughly two-thirds, or approximately $164 million of that money, will go toward players who are 34 or older, including household names such as Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber, and Zack Wheeler.

All three had quality seasons in 2026, but it's fair to question whether this team has reached its ceiling. Wheeler is entering his age-37 season, while Harper and Schwarber are entering their age-34 seasons. That figure above doesn't account for Trea Turner, an aging shortstop who will turn 34 in June, or Aaron Nola, who also turns 34 that month. Turner and Nola will make a combined $51.8 million in 2027.

"Right now we need an outfielder," said Dombrowski. "You're talking about an outfielder, you're talking about some right-handed hitting, a utility infielder, a bit more in the bullpen."

Can Dombrowski do it all? Especially in a market and a game that is defined by uncertainty this offseason?

"I don't know," he said. "It might be hard because they all cost money, too."

Whether it's through free agency, trades, or both remains to be determined. If the Phillies do spend in free agency, Seiya Suzuki remains on the Phillies' shortlist of possible options.

Despite the unpredictability surrounding the 2027 season and Philadelphia's financial commitments to aging players, Dombrowski acknowledged that owner John Middleton remains willing to spend if the right opportunity presents itself.

Still, building from within provided a good amount of the tenor during Dombrowski's media availability. The Phillies' leader was adamant regarding infield prospect Aidan Miller, intimating that the 22-year-old is certainly a real possibility as a key contributor — even more so with the struggles of Turner at shortstop in 2026.

"I really am not going to ever anoint a young player a position," Dombrowski said. "I do think he has the capabilities, and it's just not me. Anybody that's seen him, and people from other organizations probably saying, 'Wow, you still have to earn the spot, but I think that, as it stands, that would be very helpful for us to have that consideration.' And frankly, I'm hoping he does. I'm not giving it to him. But I'm hoping that he does."

A fellow should-be NL East contender is connected to the best free agent on the market.

Left-hander Tarik Skubal will reportedly meet with the Mets next week. The incumbent Dodgers, according to general manager Brandon Gomes, have also been in contact with Skubal. The expectation is that those two sides will meet at some point as well, Gomes said at the GM Meetings Tuesday. While other teams, including the Padres are expected to make a run at Skubal, the Mets and Dodgers are currently viewed as the frontrunners.

The Mets are coming off an abysmal season, finishing at the bottom of the National League East with a 74-88 record. Surely the club is in need of starting pitching, posting a 4.47 rotation ERA, the seventh-worst mark in baseball. David Stearns, the Mets president of baseball operations, elected not to comment on the Skubal sweepstakes, a customary practice this time of year, but spoke around the team's needs.

"Having a complete rotation is really important, and that includes having pitchers who can successfully get you through a postseason and get you through a playoff series," Stearns said. "We've seen over and over again in the playoffs that that can be constructed in a variety of different ways, and so we're open to doing it in any way possible."

Skubal, certainly, would offer New York an anchor to its rotation. An ace that the Mets haven't seen since Jacob deGrom. But he isn't a sudden fix to all of the Mets' pitching woes. Unquestionably, talented depth also stands at the forefront of some of the team's needs.

The club traded Freddy Peralta to the Rays at the deadline after a bad first half with New York. He turned a corner once he got with the Rays and helped lead them to a World Series. Also at the deadline, the club traded Clay Holmes, a converted starter, to the Cubs.

Both pitchers are now free agents. Meanwhile, Kodai Senga and Sean Manaea, two veterans who have underperformed in recent years, are set to become free agents after the 2027 season (Senga has a $15 million option for 2028 that will likely be declined).

Skubal is a logical fit in Queens, especially if Steve Cohen is ready to open his wallet.

"Every situation is unique," Stearns said. "It's been well-publicized, even since I've been here, we've engaged in extremely long-term negotiations for pitchers. We will do so again, but the situation matters. The specific circumstances matter. We do have to look at every individual pitcher on a case-by-case basis."

#2604. Paul George explains why he gave one 'a--hole' 76ers fan the middle finger during impressive return to Philly

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Most of the attention going into Tuesday's clash between the Eastern Conference's top two seeds went to Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown. The two former Boston Celtics teammates squared off for the first time since the latter was traded to the Philadelphia 76ers, and based on both the back and forth between them in the press and the chilly reception Brown gave Tatum on the floor, there's a fair bit of animosity between the two.

Yet it was ultimately the other player involved in that blockbuster, Paul George, who wound up stealing the show. After two years in Philadelphia, George returned to his old stomping grounds for the first time as a Celtic and led all scorers with 36 points in Boston's 123-101 victory.

Despite that stellar outing, it was what happened during a stoppage in the fourth quarter that became one of the night's most notable moments. After drilling his fourth 3-pointer to give the Celtics a 100-82 lead, the 76ers called timeout. As George retreated to Boston's bench, he gave the Philadelphia crowd the middle finger.

Looks like Paul George may have also flipped out a fan (or someone) after that three pic.twitter.com/LecXldKldE

In the moment, it felt as if George might be taking some revenge against the team that shipped him out over the summer. As George explained after the game, however, it wasn't anger at the entire 76ers fanbase or the team itself that motivated the middle finger. It was one fan in particular.

"There was a fan being an asshole," George explained. "Ball rolled to him. He looked me dead in my eyes, dropped the ball on the ground as if like I'm a dog to go fetch or go get it instead of passing the ball to me like a normal fan would do, and so yeah, so then I rolled him a middle finger in return."

Philadelphia's fans aren't known for being especially kind to opposing players, and George's tenure in Philadelphia didn't exactly go as planned. After signing a four-year max contract in the summer of 2024, George, due to a combination of injuries and a suspension, played just 78 regular-season games for the 76ers. Most of that time was spent playing below his typical standard, though he thrived after returning from that 25-game suspension a year ago and wound up being vital in Philadelphia's first-round comeback against Boston.

Now that George is thriving for a rival, there was seemingly some bitterness in the crowd. And George made it perfectly clear how he felt about that both during the game and after it.

#2602. Corey Seager landing spots: Six possible destinations with Rangers veteran on the trading block

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

A new star-quality trade candidate recently barged onto the scene in Major League Baseball. The Texas Rangers are reportedly fielding and considering trade offers for veteran shortstop Corey Seager.

The Rangers signed Corey Seager to a 10-year, $325 million deal prior to the 2022 season, and that splash signing played a leading role in the Rangers' 2023 World Series triumph. Seager was named MVP of that World Series, and during the regular season he enjoyed perhaps the best campaign of his standout career. Now, though, with the Rangers facing an uncertain future, they may be looking to unload Seager and the five years and roughly $155 million left on his pact.

It won't be simple. Seager is going into his age-33 campaign in 2027, and he suffered a downturn at the plate this past season (while still remaining a plus at the plate and in the field). As well, he's been injury-prone for much of his 12-year career. Over the last four years, he's averaged 111.5 games per season, and in recent times he's been limited by injuries to his thumb, hip, back, and both hamstrings. At his age and after such a long history of health issues, there's no reason to think that will change. Additionally, Seager can control the process. While his contract included a limited no-trade clause that allowed him to block trades to eight teams of his choosing, Seager has now earned "10 and 5" rights – i.e., he's spent at least 10 seasons in the majors and the last five with the same team – which means he has the right to block any trade.

All that said, Seager is no doubt appealing to teams in contending mode and in need of upgrades on the left side of the infield. He still has strong quality-of-contact indicators at the plate, and he's still an asset with the glove. It's easy to dream on that career OPS+ of 135 from the shortstop position and the fact that he was at peak, at least when he was on the field, as recently as 2025. The Rangers are also presumably willing to pay down a chunk of his remaining commitment in order to make a trade more tenable. As for Seager's druthers, it's possible he'd like to play out his contract for a team better positioned to deliver to him a third career World Series ring.

With all those considerations laid out, let's have a look at a handful of teams who may – or at least should – be kicking the tires on a Seager trade. We'll proceed in taut and suspenseful alphabetical order …

The Braves made it to the NLDS this past season and have made the playoffs in eight of the last nine years. For much of that time, though, they've struggled to find a reliable presence at shortstop. This past season, Atlanta shortstops combined to bat just .222/.280/.322, which is squarely in "unacceptable liability" territory. As well, the top two turn-takers at the position, Mauricio Dubón and Ha-Seong Kim, are both free agents.

Boston still has Trevor Story under contract through next season with a club option for 2028. However, Story, who soon turns 34, appears to be very much in decline, and that's in addition to his troubles staying healthy. This past season, he had an OPS+ of just 75 and was barely above replacement level overall. The Sox have signaled they're open to an upgrade at the position, and Seager would certainly be that.

Why not a headline-grabbing reunion in L.A.? Seager was a Dodgers lifer before he inked that big contract with Texas, and that level of familiarity – plus the Dodgers' ongoing excellence – could be alluring. The Dodgers could also use an upgrade in the middle infield. They could install Seager at short and shift Mookie Betts to second base, where he has significant experience. Or they could keep Betts at short, where he's adapted so very well, and let Seager transition to second – a marginally less taxing position that might even help him stay on the field. Tommy Edman, meanwhile, would transition back to a super-utility role. Either way, it's a compelling theoretical fit.

The Yankees have previously shown trade interest in Seager, so it's no great leap to think they still might be eyeing him from afar. Young George Lombard Jr. is the shortstop of the present and future in the Bronx, so Seager would likely need to be willing to shift to third base if a Yankees trade is to come to pass. The Yanks have already signaled they're ready for an upgrade over Ryan McMahon, who's been frankly terrible at the plate since being acquired from the Rockies. The lefty-swinging Seager doubtless would enjoy that short porch in right at Yankee Stadium.

Trea Turner is signed through 2033, but defensively he's become unplayable at the shortstop position. No surprise, then, that the Phillies are open to moving him, perhaps to the outfield, and finding someone else to man the critical position of short. Seager would be a needle-moving addition for lead operator Dave Dombrowski as he attempts to keep the Phils' contending window open for a bit longer. There's an argument that this would make the Philly lineup too left-handed, but the potential upgrade over what Turner provided them this past season makes it a worthwhile sacrifice.

The Jays had one of the worst offenses in all of baseball last season, and that lack of punch was the leading culprit in their tumble from the heights of 2025. Seager could be installed at short or second, and from there the Jays could shuffle infield incumbents Andrés Giménez and Ernie Clement. Indeed, Clement is perhaps at his most valuable when he's deployed as a heavily used multi-positional talent.
